narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'my eye wastes away because of grief' - the eye named not as an organ of sight but as the visible register of inner ruin. Type (102) is a state, not an act: a condition the sufferer is in, the wasting itself. Source (103) is absent - the reading books no separate origin behind the wasting, though the verse itself hangs it on grief and foes; the row reports the condition, not a traced supply, so the sorrow that drives it is left as the surrounding air rather than a named intake. Seat (104) resolves to none: for all that 'eye' is a bodily part, the operation is not treated as organ-located - the eye reads as the whole grieving self showing through, not a faculty switched on. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred): the first-person interior of the weary man who floods his bed with tears night after night. Operation (106) is the core event - 'the eye itself grows weak and wastes away because of grief and the foes', sorrow consuming the body's sight; the inner grief is eating outward into the flesh. Target (107) is grief-consumption (inferred): what the operation moves toward is not another person but the consuming itself, the interior wearing the body down. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked; the wasting is stated flatly, without qualifier of speed or struggle, the bare fact of an eye failing. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are all absent: no degree of the wasting is scored, nothing narrows it further, and no downstream result is booked - the reading holds it as a raw condition, not measured and not followed to an outcome. Coupling (112) is 'eye-wastes' (inferred): the one binding registered is the weld of the eye to its own wasting - grief and the failing eye are inseparable, the sorrow and its bodily sign one thing. Prohibition (113) is absent - this is lament, not a forbidding. Discovery (114) names the placement: 'my eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes' - the interior sorrow written on the failing eye, grief eating the body. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing condition of the sufferer, not a passing flicker. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the whole thing sits inside as a condition of the inner life, surfacing on the body. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the psalmist's grief consumes him until it shows in a wasting, weakening eye - an inner state of sorrow, welded to its own bodily wasting, aimed at nothing but the consuming itself, held wholly within and made visible in the flesh.
narratives.story: This is a psalm soaked in tears. Night after night the sufferer floods his bed with weeping, and by the end you can see what the grief has cost him: his eye is wasting away, growing weak from sheer sorrow and from the enemies that press on him. The eye here is not really about seeing - it is the place where all his inner misery shows up on the outside. His grief has begun to eat into his very body. The psalm does not explain where the sorrow first came from or where it is heading; it simply reports a man so worn by weeping that his eyes are failing. The sorrow and the wasting eye are one and the same thing - the inner ache made visible in flesh. It is a plain, unflinching picture of a heart in pain wearing the body down.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'my life is spent with sorrow' - life named as something used up, drained away. Type (102) is a state: the settled condition of depletion, not a single deed. Source (103) is absent - the reading does not book a separate origin for the spending, though the verse names sorrow, sighing, and iniquity around it; the row reports the wornness itself, leaving its precise supply unfiled. Seat (104) is none: the depletion is not organ-located - it is the whole self worn thin, not one interior organ failing. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred): the besieged, forgotten sufferer of the psalm, a man who has become 'like a broken vessel'. Operation (106) is the core event - 'the self's life is spent with sorrow, its years with sighing, strength failing through iniquity, bones wasting', a whole life eroded by grief; the inner sorrow is grinding the person down across time. Target (107) is erosion (inferred): what the operation moves toward is the wearing-away itself, the slow using-up of the man. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked; the spending is stated flatly, without qualifier. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are all absent: no degree is scored beyond 'spent', nothing narrows it, and no separate outcome is booked - the depletion simply is his state, not followed to a filed consequence. Coupling (112) is 'life-spent-sorrow' (inferred): the binding is the weld of life to sorrow - the years and the sighing are one, the vitality and its grief inseparable. Notably the verse itself ties the failing strength to 'my iniquity', so guilt sits inside this erosion as a named cause of the wearing-down. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'my life is spent with sorrow, and my years with sighing; my strength fails... and my bones waste away' - depletion over time, the interior and the body worn down by prolonged grief. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing condition of the sufferer, not a momentary dip. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the wearing-out is a condition of the inner life, felt within as the draining of the man's own vitality. The full process: from no booked source and no organ-seat, the psalmist's years are used up in sorrow and sighing, his strength failing because of his iniquity, his bones wasting - an inner state of total depletion, welded to grief, aimed at nothing but the erosion itself, held wholly within as a life spent thin.
narratives.story: The man in this psalm is besieged, slandered, and forgotten - he says he has become like a broken clay pot that people throw away. And when he describes what the long trouble has done to him, the word is spent: his whole life has been used up in sorrow, his years drained away in sighing. His strength has failed, and he plainly links that failure to his own wrongdoing; even his bones feel worn out. This is not a sudden blow but a slow grinding-down over years, sorrow eating away at both his spirit and his body until there is little left. The psalm does not tidy it up or point to where it will end; it simply lets us see a person worn thin by grief and guilt, his vitality quietly spent. The sorrow and the wasted life are the same thing - a man used up from the inside.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'my iniquities a burden too heavy' (avon) - guilt named as a physical weight. Type (102) is a state: the condition of being loaded down, not an act of sinning. Source (103) is absent - the reading books no origin behind the guilt itself; the row reports the felt mass, not where the sin came from, leaving the load standing on its own weight. Seat (104) is none: the burden is not organ-located - it presses on the whole self, not a single inner organ. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred): the sick, groaning sufferer whose flesh has 'no soundness' because of his sin. Operation (106) is the core event - 'the self's iniquities have gone over its head; like a heavy burden they are too heavy for it', the crushing weight of guilt; the movement is downward pressure, sin bearing the person down. Target (107) is guilt's-weight (inferred): what the operation moves toward is the being-crushed itself, the interior pressed under a load it cannot carry. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked; the crushing is stated flatly. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are all absent: though the verse says the load is 'too heavy', no separate degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and no downstream outcome is booked apart from the weight itself - the reading holds the mass, not a filed result. Coupling (112) is 'iniquities-burden' (inferred): the binding is the weld of iniquities to burden - guilt and unbearable weight are one image, the sin felt precisely as mass. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me' - the felt mass of sin, the interior pressed under a load it cannot carry. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing condition of the guilty sufferer. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the burden is a condition of the inner life, the sin felt as weight within. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the psalmist's guilt rises over his head and settles as a crushing weight too heavy to lift - an inner state in which sin is experienced as sheer mass, welded to the image of an unbearable burden, aimed at nothing but the crushing itself, held wholly within as guilt that bears the whole person down.
narratives.story: This is the prayer of a man whose body is breaking down and who knows why: his sin has made him sick. When he speaks of his wrongdoing, he does not describe a deed so much as a weight. His guilt, he says, has risen up over his head like flood-water, and it lies on him like a load far too heavy to carry. It is not something he can shrug off; it presses him down, crushing him. The psalm does not trace where the sin began or where the weight will go - it simply lets us feel the mass of it, guilt experienced as sheer heaviness that bears a person to the ground. His sin and that unbearable weight are one and the same. It is one of the most physical pictures of guilt there is: a man buckling under a load he cannot lift off his own back.
narratives.variation_note: This is one of eight distinct readings of avon rendered 'iniquities' across the Psalter, and its difference is the finding: here at Psa 38:4 the guilt is read as a crushing WEIGHT borne by the guilty man himself, felt as unbearable mass. It stands apart from the pleaded-erasure readings (Psa 51:9 'blot out all'), the confessed-ancestral guilt (Psa 79:8), the guilt exposed before God (Psa 90:8), the guilt God graciously does not repay (Psa 103:10), the guilt that issues in affliction (Psa 107:17), and the reckoning-and-redemption pair of Psa 130 (v3, v8). Where those weigh iniquity as something confessed, erased, or judged, this one weighs it as felt burden - sin known first by its sheer heaviness on the one who bears it.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'heal me, for I have sinned against you' (chata) - sin named inside a plea for healing. Type (102) is cognition: not a bare deed here but an act of the knowing self, sin owned and confessed rather than done. Source (103) is absent - the reading books no origin behind the sinning; the row reports the confession, not the sin's supply. Seat (104) is none: the confessing is not organ-located - it is the whole self owning its fault, not an interior organ. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred): the sick man of the psalm who, unlike his malicious enemies, turns his sickness Godward. Operation (106) is the core event - 'the self asks God to be gracious and heal it, confessing that it has sinned against him', healing sought with confession; the movement joins petition to admission. Target (107) is penitent-plea (inferred): what the operation aims at is the plea itself, the asking-while-owning, directed to God. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked; the confession stands plainly, without qualifier of anguish or degree. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are all absent: no degree of the sin is scored, nothing narrows it, and no downstream result is booked - the reading holds the confessing act, not a filed outcome. Coupling (112) is 'heal-me-i-sinned' (inferred): the binding is the weld of healing to confession - the request for grace and the owning of sin are one utterance, the sufferer refusing to plead innocence. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'O Lord, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you!' - petition joined to confession; the interior does not claim innocence but asks healing while owning its sin. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing posture of the penitent, not a passing impulse. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the confessing is a condition of the inner life, the self's owning of its fault held within. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the psalmist turns his sickness into confession, asking God for grace and healing in the very breath in which he admits he has sinned - an inner act of penitent knowing, welded to the plea for mercy, aimed at God, held within as the honest owning of a fault the sufferer will not deny.
narratives.story: Surrounded by enemies who whisper that he is finished, this sick man does something they never do: he turns to God and tells the truth about himself. His prayer is simple - be gracious to me, heal me - but he does not stop there. In the same breath he adds the reason he needs mercy: I have sinned against you. He does not protest his innocence or blame his troubles on others; he owns his fault even as he asks to be made well. Asking for grace and admitting his sin are, for him, a single act. The psalm does not measure how bad the sin was or say what became of it - it simply shows a man who, when he is at his lowest, does not hide behind excuses but lays his wrongdoing honestly before God and asks to be healed. That plain, unflinching honesty is the heart of the moment.
narratives.variation_note: Among the five readings of chata 'sinned', this one at Psa 41:4 is coded as COGNITION - sin owned in a confession joined to a plea for healing, the self honestly admitting its fault. It differs from the vertical confession of Psa 51:4 ('against you only have I sinned', locus external to God), and sharply from the two Asaph readings where the same word is an ACTION of persistent rebellion ('they sinned still more', Psa 78:17; 'they still sinned', Psa 78:32) and from the corporate confession of Psa 106:6 ('we and our fathers have sinned'). The difference tracks bearer and stance: here a single penitent owning his sin to seek healing, there a people sinning against God despite mercy and judgment, or a nation confessing across generations.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the iniquity of those who cheat me' (avon) - guilt located not in the psalmist but in his defrauders. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition of the wicked, not a deed the psalmist does. Source (103) is absent - the reading books no origin behind the cheaters' iniquity; the row reports the encircling wrong, not its root. Seat (104) is none: the iniquity is not organ-located - it is the supplanters' condition, not an interior organ. Bearer (105), crucially, is 'those who cheat/supplant' (inferred) - the interior held here is the wealthy defrauders', read from the outside as menace. Operation (106) is 'surround' (inferred): the event is the encircling itself, the wicked's iniquity closing round the psalmist like a besieging ring. Target (107) is the psalmist (inferred): the iniquity is aimed at him - he is the one it surrounds. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked; the encircling is stated flatly. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are all absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and no downstream outcome is booked - the reading holds the surrounding menace, not a filed result. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'the iniquity the psalmist need not fear' - the wrong is welded to the psalm's opening question, 'Why should I fear in times of trouble?'; the encircling guilt is bound precisely to the fearlessness that sees through it. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'the iniquity of those who cheat me surrounds me' - the encircling wickedness of the supplanters; the iniquity of wealthy defrauders whose menace the wise sees through, knowing their end. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the cheaters. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the iniquity is a condition of their inner life, even as it surrounds another. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the defrauders' iniquity closes round the psalmist as a besieging menace - yet the reading welds that encircling guilt to the psalmist's refusal to fear, for he sees the wicked's end (they die like beasts, their wealth left behind). This is the family read in its social, threatening form: iniquity as the surrounding pressure of the rich and ruthless, which the wise interior faces without dread.
narratives.story: This psalm opens with a defiant question: why should I be afraid, even when the wrongdoing of those who cheat me closes in on all sides? Here the guilt does not belong to the speaker but to the ruthless, wealthy men pressing around him - people who trust in their money and boast about their riches. Their wickedness surrounds him like a besieging army, and it is aimed squarely at him. Yet the whole point of the psalm is that he refuses to be frightened by it, because he can see where such people end up: rich or not, they die like the beasts, carrying nothing away, their fine houses left to strangers and their names forgotten. So the menace is real and it encircles him, but it has no power to make him afraid, because he understands its limit. It is a picture of guilt as the crowding threat of the powerful - and of a clear-eyed heart that looks straight through it.
narratives.variation_note: This is one of nine readings of avon 'iniquity', and it is the outlier in bearer: here at Psa 49:5 the iniquity belongs to the WICKED (the defrauders), read as an external menace that surrounds the psalmist, whereas most avon readings place the guilt on the penitent self or God's people (washed in Psa 51:2, inborn in Psa 51:5, atoned in Psa 78:38, forgiven in Psa 85:2). The difference is a shift of both bearer and stance - not guilt confessed and cleansed, but guilt faced without fear because the wise interior already knows the wicked's end.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is pesha - 'blot out my transgressions', rebellion, the willful breach. Type (102) is a status: the standing condition of being in rebellion, named to be erased. Source (103) carries a span-resolved value - the plea is 'appealed against God's steadfast love and abundant mercy (v1)'; the transgression's answer is sourced not in the self but in divine mercy, the penitent grounding his whole appeal on God's character. Seat (104) is none: the rebellion is not organ-located - it belongs to the whole person, not an interior organ. Bearer (105) is the penitent (David, inferred): the first-person breaker of covenant who opens the psalm. Operation (106) is 'confessed / owned, pleaded blotted out' (inferred): the event is the owning-and-erasing plea, the interior naming its rebellion and asking it wiped away. Target (107) is 'against God' (inferred): the transgression is directed at God himself; even a wrong against people is read as breach against him. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked; the plea stands plainly. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are all absent: no degree of the rebellion is scored, nothing narrows it, and no downstream result is booked - the reading holds the confessing plea, not a filed outcome. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: pesha is 'named again in the confession (v3)' - the transgression of v1 is welded to its re-acknowledgement, 'I know my transgressions'; the plea and the self-knowledge are bound together. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions' - the penitent owns his rebellion and pleads it erased; pesha is the first of the sin-triad (pesha / avon / chatta't) David lays before God, appealing only to divine mercy. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the penitent's condition. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the rebellion is a condition of the inner life, owned within. The full process: from a source that is God's own mercy rather than the self, and with no organ-seat, the penitent names his rebellion - his willful breach against God - and pleads it blotted out, welding this opening confession to its later re-acknowledgement, holding the transgression wholly within as the first of three words by which he lays his whole guilt before a merciful God.
narratives.story: This is the great psalm of repentance, and its very first words go straight to the heart of the matter. David does not begin with excuses; he begins with a plea for mercy and asks God to blot out his rebellions - his deliberate breaking of what he owed to God. And notice where he anchors his hope: not in anything good in himself, but entirely in God's steadfast love and abundant mercy. The wrong is real and he names it as rebellion, an act aimed ultimately against God. He will say it again a moment later - 'I know my transgressions' - so this is no slip of the tongue but a settled, honest owning of who he has been. He asks only one thing: that this rebellion be wiped clean away. It is the opening move of a man who has stopped defending himself and thrown his whole case on the mercy of the God he has wronged.
narratives.variation_note: This is one of six readings of pesha 'transgression'. Here at Psa 51:1 it is the penitent's OWN rebellion, confessed and pleaded blotted out on the ground of God's mercy - the opening of the sin-triad. It differs from its twin at Psa 51:3 (the same rebellion acknowledged as self-knowledge, 'I know my transgressions'), from the disavowed transgression of Psa 59:3 (the psalmist protesting he has none), from the transgression God himself atones at Psa 65:3, from the sons' transgression met with the rod at Psa 89:32, and from the transgression removed 'as far as east from west' at Psa 103:12. The same word runs from owned rebellion, through denied guilt, to divine erasure - the arc itself is the finding.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is avon - 'wash me thoroughly from my iniquity', the crookedness or ingrained guilt. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition of the self, deeper than a single act. Source (103) is absent - the reading books no origin here; that this iniquity reaches back to birth is stated later (v5), but this row reports the plea, not the root. Seat (104) is none: the iniquity is not organ-located - it stains the whole self, not one organ. Bearer (105) is the penitent (inferred): David asking to be cleansed. Operation (106) is 'pleaded washed away' (inferred): the event is the plea for cleansing, the interior asking to be scrubbed of its guilt. Target (107) is none: the reading books no object the iniquity is aimed at - it is not directed outward but held as the penitent's own condition to be washed. Manner (108) carries a value - 'thoroughly / abundantly' (inferred): the how is marked, an intensified cleansing; the guilt is deep enough that ordinary rinsing will not do. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no separate degree is scored, nothing further narrows it, and no downstream outcome is booked - the 'thoroughly' lives in the manner, not a filed result. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'the deep-rooted guilt named again (v5, v9)' - the iniquity of v2 is welded to its recurrences, the inborn iniquity of v5 and the 'all my iniquities' of v9; one guilt tracked across the psalm. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity' - the crookedness the penitent begs cleansed; avon the ingrained perversity, deeper than a single act, needing washing, not mere pardon. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the penitent's condition. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the iniquity is a condition of the inner life, a stain within. The full process: from an unnamed source but a guilt the psalm will trace to birth, and with no organ-seat, the penitent asks to be washed thoroughly of an ingrained crookedness that is not a passing deed but a settled stain - a guilt deep enough to need scrubbing not just pardon, held wholly within, welded to its own recurrences across the prayer.
narratives.story: Right after asking God to blot out his rebellion, David reaches for a different picture: washing. 'Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity,' he prays - and the word thoroughly matters. He is not describing a single bad act that could be simply excused; he is describing something soaked deep into him, a crookedness that ordinary rinsing will not shift. He will admit a few lines later that it goes all the way back to his birth, and he will return to it again, begging God to wipe out all of it. So this is guilt understood as a stain that has set into the fabric of the person, needing a deep cleansing rather than a quick pardon. He holds it as his own condition, not something out there to be dealt with, and he asks God to scrub him clean. It is the honesty of a man who knows his problem is not just what he did, but what he is.
narratives.variation_note: Within the nine avon 'iniquity' readings, this one at Psa 51:2 is guilt as an INGRAINED STAIN the penitent begs washed away, marked by the manner 'thoroughly'. It is the head of a chain the psalm itself follows - the same avon reappears at Psa 51:5 (traced to conception) and Psa 51:9 ('all' of it blotted). It differs from the encircling menace of the wicked (Psa 49:5), the crushing burden (Psa 38:4), and the guilt God forgives or does not repay (Psa 85:2; Psa 103:10): here iniquity is a deep personal defilement requiring cleansing, not pardon alone.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chatta't - 'cleanse me from my sin', the missing of the mark, the concrete failure. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition to be cleansed, not the act of sinning here. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the plea, not the sin's root. Seat (104) is none: the sin is not organ-located - it stains the whole self. Bearer (105) is the penitent (inferred): David. Operation (106) is 'confessed' (inferred): the event is the owning of the failure in the plea for cleansing. Target (107) is none: the reading books no object - the sin is held as the penitent's own condition, not aimed outward. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree, nothing narrowing, no downstream outcome - just the failure named. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'the third of the sin-triad, ever before him (v3)' - the sin of v2 is welded to its recurrence in v3, where the penitent says 'my sin is ever before me'; the cleansing-plea and the constant self-view are bound. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'cleanse me from my sin!' - the missing-of-the-mark completing the triad (pesha / avon / chatta't); the concrete failure the penitent names, which he says is 'ever before me' (v3), sin held constantly in view, not suppressed. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the penitent's condition. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the sin is a condition of the inner life, held within. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the penitent names his concrete failure - the third and completing word of his confession - and asks it cleansed, welding this plea to the admission that the sin is always before his eyes; a failure owned as his own inner condition, held wholly within and never looked away from.
narratives.story: David has now used two words for what is wrong with him - rebellion and ingrained crookedness - and here he adds the third and most ordinary: sin, a plain falling-short, a missing of the mark. 'Cleanse me from my sin,' he asks. What is striking is what he says next: this sin is 'ever before me' - always in his sight, never pushed out of mind. He does not bury it or try to forget it; he keeps looking straight at it even as he asks God to wash it away. So together with the earlier words, this completes his honest naming of the whole problem. It is his own failure, held as his own condition, and he refuses to let it out of view. That steady, unflinching gaze at his own wrong is exactly the mark of real repentance - a man who will not excuse himself and will not look away.
narratives.variation_note: This is one of six readings of chatta't/chattath 'sin'. Here at Psa 51:2 it is the penitent's OWN concrete failure, pleaded cleansed and kept 'ever before' him (v3) - one of a matched pair with the very next verse. It differs from the enemies' sin located in their mouths (Psa 59:12), the people's sin owned in an appeal for atonement (Psa 79:9), the sin God covered (Psa 85:2), and the invoked, unblotted sin of an enemy's mother (Psa 109:14). The same word runs from a penitent's honest self-view to a curse called down on another's guilt - bearer and stance make the difference.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chatta't - 'my sin is ever before me', the failure held constantly in view. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition, the sin as something continually present. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the constant seeing, not the sin's root. Seat (104) is none: the sin is not organ-located - it is the whole self's condition kept before the whole self. Bearer (105) is the penitent (inferred): David. Operation (106) is 'held ever before him' (inferred): the event is the keeping-in-view, the interior refusing to look away from its failure. Target (107) is none: the reading books no external object - the sin is turned back on the self as the thing perpetually seen. Manner (108) carries a value - 'continually (ever before me)' (inferred): the how is marked as unbroken, constant; the sin is not glimpsed and dismissed but steadily faced. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome is booked - the reading holds the constant view, not a filed result. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'the chatta't he begged cleansed (v2)' - the sin of v3 is welded to the cleansing-plea of v2; the constant self-view and the plea for washing are one motion. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'and my sin is ever before me' - sin kept constantly in view, not repressed; the mark of true contrition, the penitent unable to look away from his failure. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the contrite interior. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the sin's constant presence is a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the penitent keeps his failure continually before him, refusing to repress or forget it - the same sin he begged cleansed in the previous line now held steadily in view, an inner state of unbroken self-facing that is the very signature of contrition.
narratives.story: David has just asked God to wash his sin away, and now he tells us something about how he is living with it in the meantime: 'my sin is ever before me.' It never leaves his sight. He does not manage his guilt by forgetting it, distracting himself, or pretending it was smaller than it was; he keeps looking straight at it, day and night, even as he begs to be cleansed. This constant, honest facing of his own failure is not despair - it is the very mark of a truly sorry heart. The same sin he wants gone he refuses to hide from. It is a quiet, powerful picture of repentance: a man who will not look away from what he has done until God himself takes it away.
narratives.variation_note: Paired with Psa 51:2, this second chatta't reading holds the SAME sin but at a different moment of the same motion: v2 pleads it cleansed, v3 keeps it 'ever before' the penitent, with the manner marked as continual. The distinction the study preserves is between the plea for removal and the settled refusal to look away - two faces of one contrition. Both differ from the other-directed and imprecatory 'sin' readings (Psa 59:12; Psa 109:14), where the guilt is another's, not the self's held in constant view.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is pesha - 'I know my transgressions', rebellion now owned in self-knowledge. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition, the rebellion acknowledged. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the acknowledgement, not the root. Seat (104) is none: the rebellion is not organ-located - it belongs to the whole person. Bearer (105) is the penitent (inferred): David. Operation (106) is 'acknowledged' (inferred): the event is the knowing-and-owning, the interior recognizing its own breach. Target (107) is none: the reading books no external object - the transgression is turned inward as the thing known. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree, nothing narrowing, no downstream outcome - just the rebellion known. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'the pesha he pleaded blotted (v1)' - the transgression of v3 is welded to the opening plea of v1; the acknowledgement and the plea for erasure are bound. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'For I know my transgressions' - the rebellion the penitent acknowledges, echoing v1; pesha owned in the light of self-knowledge, no longer hidden but confessed. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the penitent's condition. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the rebellion is a condition of the inner life, now brought to knowledge within. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the penitent turns knowledge on himself and owns his rebellion - the very breach he had pleaded blotted out in v1 now consciously acknowledged, no longer hidden but held in the clear light of self-knowledge; rebellion faced, not denied, within.
narratives.story: David opened by asking God to wipe out his rebellions; now he explains why he can pray that way: 'I know my transgressions.' He is not confessing in a vague, general way - he sees clearly what he has done, and he owns it. There is no hiding left in him, no pretending it was someone else's fault or that he does not really understand what happened. He has brought his own rebellion into full view and taken responsibility for it. This clear-eyed self-knowledge is the ground of everything else in the psalm: because he truly knows his sin, he can truly ask for it to be taken away. It is the honesty of a man who has stopped running from himself.
narratives.variation_note: This second pesha reading is the twin of Psa 51:1: the same rebellion, but where v1 PLEADS it blotted out on the ground of mercy, v3 ACKNOWLEDGES it in self-knowledge ('I know my transgressions'). The difference the study keeps is between petition and recognition - the plea and the clear owning that grounds it. Both stand apart from the disavowed transgression of Psa 59:3, the God-atoned transgression of Psa 65:3, the rod-punished transgression of Psa 89:32, and the far-removed transgression of Psa 103:12.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chata - 'against you, you only, have I sinned', the act of missing the mark confessed vertically. Type (102) is an action: a doing, the deed of sinning owned. Source (103) carries a span-resolved value - the sin is 'confessed so that God is shown justified when he judges (v4)'; the confession's purpose is booked to God's vindication, the penitent owning his act precisely so that God's verdict stands clear. Seat (104) is none: the sinning is not organ-located - it is the whole self's deed. Bearer (105) is the penitent (inferred): David. Operation (106) is 'sinned' (inferred): the event is the sin itself, now confessed. Target (107) is 'against God (you only)' (inferred): the deed is directed at God - though David wronged Bathsheba and Uriah, the reading books the ultimate target as God alone. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no separate outcome booked. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is paired with 'done what is evil in your sight' - the sinning is welded to the doing of evil before God's eyes; the act and its evil quality are one, and both are before God. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight' - the vertical reckoning of sin; though David wronged people, all sin is ultimately against God, chata confessed so that God is justified in his verdict (v4b, the qualifier). Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the penitent's confession. Locus (116) is external:god - and this is the sharp finding: the sin's reference-point is not the human victims but God himself; the deed is measured against God, not merely against those it harmed. The full process: from a source booked to God's own vindication, and with no organ-seat, the penitent confesses his deed as aimed 'against you only' - collapsing the horizontal harm into a wrong that is ultimately against God, welded to the evil done in God's sight, its whole reference external to God, so that in owning the act the penitent leaves God's judgment blameless.
narratives.story: This is one of the most startling lines in the whole psalm. David's sin harmed real people - Bathsheba, her husband Uriah, others - and yet he prays, 'Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight.' He is not denying that he hurt anyone; he is saying that at its deepest level every wrong he did was ultimately an offence against God. He measures his sin not first by the damage to others but by God, before whom it was done. And he owns it for a striking reason: so that God is shown completely in the right when he passes judgment. There is no self-defence here, no attempt to soften the verdict; by confessing fully, David leaves God's justice unblemished. It is the confession of a man who has understood that his real reckoning is with God himself.
narratives.variation_note: Among the five chata 'sinned' readings, this one at Psa 51:4 is the VERTICAL confession - sin as a deed owned as ultimately 'against God only', its locus fixed external to God and its purpose God's vindication. It differs from the healing-plea confession of Psa 41:4 (cognition, locus internal), the persistent rebellion of Psa 78:17 and Psa 78:32 (sin mounting against mercy and judgment), and the corporate confession of Psa 106:6. The finding is the collapse of horizontal harm into a wrong measured against God - a stance unique to this reading.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chet - 'in sin did my mother conceive me', sinfulness reaching back to conception. Type (102) is a status: an inborn condition, not a chosen act. Source (103) is absent - no separate origin is booked behind it; indeed the point of the reading is that the sin has no later starting-point, it is there from the beginning. Seat (104) is none: the sin is not organ-located - it is the whole self's native condition. Bearer (105) is the penitent from conception (inferred): David, traced back to his very origin. Operation (106) is 'conceived in' (inferred): the event is the being-conceived-in-sin, the interior formed already inside a sinful condition. Target (107) is none: the reading books no object - this is a condition, not a deed aimed anywhere. Manner (108) carries a value - 'from conception' (inferred): the how marks the reach of the condition, its backward extent to the moment of origin. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing further narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is paired with 'brought forth in iniquity' - the sin of v5b is welded to the iniquity of v5a; native sin and native iniquity are one confession of inborn corruption. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'and in sin did my mother conceive me' - sinfulness reaching back to conception; chet the inborn bent, completing the confession of native corruption that makes the plea for re-creation (v10) necessary. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing, constitutional trait. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the sin is a condition of the inner life, present from the first. The full process: from no later source - because it has none - and no organ-seat, the penitent traces his sin all the way back to conception, confessing a bent that was in him before he ever acted, welded to the parallel confession of inborn iniquity; a native corruption held wholly within, which is exactly why, a few lines on, he must ask God not to reform him but to create in him a clean heart.
narratives.story: David goes further back than his adult failures - further back than any single choice - and makes an astonishing admission: 'in sin did my mother conceive me.' He is saying the problem was there from the very start, before he had done anything at all; a bent toward wrong was woven into him from conception. This is not an excuse - he is not blaming his birth to escape responsibility. It is a deeper confession: the trouble is not just what he did, but what he has been all along. And it explains the extraordinary prayer that follows a little later, when he asks God to 'create in me a clean heart.' A man who saw his sin as only a few bad acts might ask to be forgiven; a man who sees it running all the way back to his origin knows he needs to be remade from the inside out.
narratives.variation_note: Among the three chet 'sins' readings, this one at Psa 51:5 is INBORN sin, traced to conception, marked by the manner 'from conception' and welded to the parallel confession of native iniquity. It differs from Psa 51:9, where the same word names the sins the penitent begs God to look away from, and from Psa 103:10, where 'our sins' are what God's mercy does not requite. Here sin is not an act to be hidden or a debt to be waived but a constitutional condition present from the first - the ground of the plea for a created clean heart.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is avon - 'I was brought forth in iniquity', guilt shown as native, dating from birth. Type (102) is a status: an inborn condition. Source (103) is absent - no later origin is booked, and that absence is itself the point: the iniquity has no acquired starting-point, it is there from birth. Seat (104) is none: the iniquity is not organ-located - it is the whole self's native condition. Bearer (105) is the penitent (inferred): David traced to his origin. Operation (106) resolves to none: the row records no event-verb - there is no act here, only the state of having been brought forth already in iniquity; the silence marks that this is condition, not deed. Target (107) is none: no object - the iniquity is aimed nowhere; it simply is his native ground. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree, nothing narrowing, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'the avon of v2, now traced to birth' - the iniquity the penitent begged washed away in v2 is welded here to its origin; the guilt and its native root are bound as one. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'I was brought forth in iniquity' - the guilt of v2 now traced to its origin; avon shown as native, not acquired, the ground of the plea for a created clean heart (v10). Role (115) is characteristic: a standing, constitutional trait. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the iniquity is a condition of the inner life, present from birth. The full process: with no operation and no aimed target - because this is not a deed but a native condition - and no source and no organ-seat, the penitent confesses that the very iniquity he asked to be washed away was in him from birth; guilt read at its deepest, not chosen but inborn, welded to the earlier cleansing-plea and held wholly within as the constitutional ground of his need to be re-created clean.
narratives.story: In the same breath as confessing he was conceived in sin, David says he was 'brought forth in iniquity' - that the crookedness he earlier begged God to wash away has been part of him since the day he was born. This reading is striking for what it does not contain: there is no action, no deed, no moment when it started. That is the whole point. This is not something David did; it is something he was, from the very beginning. The iniquity he wanted scrubbed clean turns out to have been there before he could choose anything. Again, this is not an alibi - it is a deeper diagnosis. It is why, moments later, he does not merely ask to be forgiven but to be made new: 'create in me a clean heart.' You cannot wash out what was woven in at birth; you can only be re-created.
narratives.variation_note: This avon reading is unique among the nine in recording NO operation - it is pure inborn state, guilt traced to birth with no deed attached, and welded back to the cleansing-plea of Psa 51:2. It differs from every action- or plea-bearing avon reading (washed in 51:2, surrounding in 49:5, atoned in 78:38, forgiven in 85:2, judged in 106:43): here iniquity is simply the ground one is born on, which is why the psalm turns from washing to re-creation.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chet - 'hide your face from my sins', the failures the penitent begs God not to look upon. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition to be un-seen. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the plea, not the sins' root. Seat (104) is none: the sins are not organ-located - they are the whole self's failures. Bearer (105) is the penitent (inferred): David. Operation (106) is 'pleaded hidden from God's sight' (inferred): the event is the request that God look away, the interior asking its sins un-regarded. Target (107) is none: the reading books no object the sins are aimed at - they are the penitent's own, offered up to be hidden. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree, nothing narrowing, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is paired with 'blot out all my iniquities' - the sins of v9a are welded to the iniquities of v9b; God's looking-away and his erasing are twinned, pardon read as both un-seeing and un-writing. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'Hide your face from my sins' - the plea that God look away from his failures; chet the sins the penitent begs God not to gaze upon, twinned with the blotting of all iniquities, pardon as both un-seeing and erasing. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the penitent's condition. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the sins are a condition of the inner life, offered to be hidden. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the penitent asks God to turn his face away from his failures and, in the same motion, to blot out all his guilt - pardon pictured as two acts welded into one, God ceasing to see and ceasing to hold on record; the sins held within, laid before God only to be un-regarded and erased.
narratives.story: By now David has named his sin honestly again and again, refusing to hide it from himself. So his prayer here is pointed: 'Hide your face from my sins.' He has looked at them squarely; now he asks God to look away. And he pairs it immediately with another request - 'blot out all my iniquities.' Together these paint forgiveness as two motions joined into one: God no longer gazing on his failures, and God wiping them off the record altogether. It is not that the sins are pretended away; David has been the most honest man in the room about them. It is that he is asking God to stop counting them against him and to erase them completely. The man who would not look away from his own guilt now begs the one he wronged to do exactly that.
narratives.variation_note: This third-in-the-psalm reading of chet at Psa 51:9 is sin offered to be UN-SEEN and erased ('hide your face'), twinned with the blotting of all iniquities. It differs from the inborn sin of Psa 51:5 (a native condition, not a thing to be hidden) and from Psa 103:10, where 'our sins' are what God does not repay. The finding is the shape of pardon here: not washing (v2) nor re-creation (v10) but God ceasing to look and ceasing to record - a distinct facet of the same forgiveness.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is avon - 'blot out all my iniquities', the total erasure of guilt sought. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition, named to be wiped away. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked here; the row reports the plea, not the root. Seat (104) is none: the iniquities are not organ-located - they belong to the whole self. Bearer (105) is the penitent (inferred): David. Operation (106) is 'pleaded blotted out' (inferred): the event is the plea for erasure, the interior asking all its guilt struck from the record. Target (107) is none: no object - the iniquities are the penitent's own, held up only to be erased. Manner (108) carries a value - 'all of them' (inferred): the how marks totality; not some but every one of his iniquities is to be wiped. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no separate degree beyond 'all' is scored, nothing further narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'the avon of v2, v5 - now all erased' - the iniquity begged washed (v2) and traced to birth (v5) is welded here to its total blotting; one guilt tracked to its complete erasure. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'and blot out all my iniquities' - the total erasure sought; avon 'all' of it, the ingrained guilt of v2/v5 pleaded wiped away completely, the negative counterpart to the created clean heart that follows (v10). Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the penitent's condition. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the iniquities are a condition of the inner life, offered for erasure. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the penitent asks that every one of his iniquities - the same ingrained guilt he begged washed and confessed as inborn - be blotted out entirely; guilt tracked from stain (v2), through native root (v5), to complete erasure here, held wholly within and offered up for total removal, the clearing-away that makes room for the clean heart to be created.
narratives.story: This is where David's confession reaches for everything to be gone. 'Blot out all my iniquities,' he prays - not some of them, not the worst of them, but all. He has traced this crookedness through the whole psalm: he begged to be washed of it, he admitted it went back to his birth, and now he asks God to strike every last bit of it off the record. The little word all carries the weight: he wants no leftover guilt, nothing held back against him. And this total erasing clears the ground for the very next thing he asks - that God create in him a clean heart. First the old record wiped completely away, then a new beginning. It is the prayer of a man who wants not a partial pardon but a completely clean slate.
narratives.variation_note: This iniquities reading at Psa 51:9 is the END of the psalm's avon chain - the same guilt washed at 51:2 and traced to birth at 51:5 now pleaded 'all' blotted out, marked by the manner 'all of them'. Within the eight 'iniquities' (avon) readings it differs from the crushing burden (Psa 38:4), the confessed ancestral guilt (Psa 79:8), the exposure before God (Psa 90:8), the mercy that withholds repayment (Psa 103:10), the affliction-bearing guilt (Psa 107:17), and the Psa 130 reckoning/redemption pair. Here the note is totality and erasure - every iniquity wiped to make room for a created clean heart.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is pasha - 'I will teach transgressors your ways', fellow rebels named as those the pardoned man will instruct. Type (102) is an action: a doing, the resolve to teach. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked behind the resolve, though the whole psalm's pardon plainly stands behind it; the row reports the intent, not its supply. Seat (104) is none: the teaching is not organ-located - it is the whole self's outward turn. Bearer (105) is double (inferred): 'the penitent (teaching) / transgressors (taught)' - the interior at issue is both the forgiven man who teaches and the rebels who are taught. Operation (106) is 'teach God's ways': the event is the instruction itself, the pardoned penitent passing on what he has learned. Target (107) is transgressors (inferred): the teaching is aimed at fellow rebels - the object is the very kind of person the penitent himself has been. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no separate outcome booked (though the next clause hopes sinners will return). Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'paired with sinners returning to God' - the teaching of transgressors is welded to the returning of sinners; instruction and repentance are bound, the one aimed at producing the other. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'Then I will teach transgressors your ways' - the pardoned penitent's resolve to help fellow rebels; the fruit of forgiveness turning outward, the one who knew his own rebellion (v1, v3) now teaching other transgressors God's ways, that sinners may return. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait, a settled resolve. Locus (116) is external:person - and this is the finding: the reference-point is not the self's inner state but other people; the pardon turns outward, its locus another human being. The full process: from no booked source but a resolve grown out of his own forgiveness, and with no organ-seat, the penitent turns from confession to mission - resolving to teach fellow rebels God's ways, welding that teaching to the hoped return of sinners, its whole reference lying outside himself in others; pardon become purpose, the man who owned his own rebellion now bending outward to reclaim other rebels.
narratives.story: Something turns here in the psalm. Up to this point David has been entirely absorbed in his own guilt - naming it, owning it, begging to be washed and remade. Now, looking ahead to being forgiven, he makes a promise that faces outward: 'I will teach transgressors your ways.' The very man who knew what it was to rebel against God now wants to help other rebels find the road back. His forgiveness does not just leave him relieved; it gives him a purpose. And he ties that teaching directly to a hope - that sinners will return to God. So the pardon that healed his own inner life immediately reaches beyond him toward other people. It is the mark of grace received turning into grace passed on: a forgiven man becoming a guide for the very kind of person he used to be.
narratives.variation_note: H6586:transgressor (pasha, 'transgressors') occurs once, but it is paired at the same verse with H2400:sinner#1 ('sinners will return'): the two must not be collapsed. This reading is the penitent's OUTWARD-turning ACTION - teaching fellow rebels God's ways, its locus fixed on other persons - while its partner is the RESULT, sinners turning back to God (locus external to God). Together they show pardon become mission: the forgiven man's deed of teaching and the repentance it aims to produce.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chatta - 'sinners will return to you', wrongdoers pictured turning back to God. Type (102) is an action: a doing, the turning itself. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked behind the return; the row reports the turning, not its spring, though the penitent's teaching is its named occasion. Seat (104) is none: the returning is not organ-located - it is the whole self's turn. Bearer (105) is sinners (inferred): the interior at issue is that of the wrongdoers who come back. Operation (106) is 'return / turn back (shub)' (inferred): the event is the turning of sinners back toward God, the reversal of a life away from him. Target (107) is 'to God' (inferred): the return is aimed at God - the sinners turn Godward. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked beyond the return itself. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'the fruit of teaching transgressors God's ways' - the sinners' return is welded to the penitent's resolve to teach; the turning is the harvest of the instruction. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'and sinners will return to you' - the repentance the penitent's testimony produces; chatta the sinners who turn back to God, the pardoned life bearing fruit in others' return, penitence become mission. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the turned life. Locus (116) is external:god - the reference-point is God, toward whom the sinners move; the return's whole orientation lies outside the self, in God. The full process: from no booked source but the occasion of the penitent's teaching, and with no organ-seat, sinners turn back to God - the reversal of lives away from him, welded to the instruction that produces it, its whole orientation Godward; the pardoned man's forgiveness bearing fruit not only in his own healing but in others' return, penitence become a mission that reaches all the way to God.
narratives.story: David's promise to teach other wrongdoers comes with a hope attached: 'and sinners will return to you.' He imagines people who have been living turned away from God actually turning back toward him - and turning back because of what David, a forgiven sinner, will tell them. This is the harvest he longs for from his own pardon. His restoration is not meant to end with himself; he pictures it spreading, so that others who have gone astray find their way home to God too. The direction of the whole thing is Godward - these sinners are moving back toward the God they had left. It is a beautiful outward reach from a psalm that began in the depths of one man's guilt: mercy received becoming mercy that draws others back.
narratives.variation_note: One of two chatta 'sinners' readings, and the redemptive one: here at Psa 51:13 sinners RETURN to God, the fruit of the penitent's teaching, oriented Godward. It stands in stark contrast to Psa 104:35, where 'sinners' are the object of an imprecation - 'let sinners be consumed from the earth'. The same noun names, in one place, wrongdoers being reclaimed, and in another, wrongdoers wished swept away; the difference between mission and judgment is the finding.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is avel - 'doing abominable iniquity', injustice or perversity as the substance of the fool's deeds. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition of the corrupt, expressed in deeds. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked, yet the verse itself names the root just before: 'The fool says in his heart, There is no God.' The reading leaves the source-row empty even though the psalm hangs the iniquity on that denial; the wrong is reported, its spring left in the surrounding text. Seat (104) is none: the iniquity is not organ-located - though 'heart' is named as where the fool denies God, the iniquity itself is not lodged in an organ but marks the whole corrupt person. Bearer (105) is the fools (inferred): the interior of those who say there is no God and are corrupt. Operation (106) is 'done' (inferred): the event is the doing of the iniquity, corruption issuing in deed. Target (107) is none: the reading books no object - the iniquity is the content of their corruption, not aimed at a named victim here. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'the iniquity that is abominable' - the avel is welded to its qualifier 'abominable'; the wrong and its loathsomeness are one, injustice named as detestable. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'doing abominable iniquity' - the injustice/perversity that is the substance of the abominable deeds; avel the moral wrong the fools practise, the concrete content of their corruption. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the fool. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the iniquity is a condition of the inner life, issuing in corrupt deeds. The full process: from a source the psalm names but the row leaves unbooked - the heart's denial of God - and with no organ-seat, the fools practise abominable iniquity; injustice as the concrete substance of their corruption, welded to its own loathsomeness, held within as a condition of a godless interior that issues in perverse deeds. This is the family read at the root: sin flowing from a heart that has first said there is no God.
narratives.story: This psalm looks at the worst kind of corruption and traces it to its source. It begins with a person who says in his heart, 'There is no God' - and from that denial everything else follows. Such people, the psalm says, are rotten through and through, and what they actually do is 'abominable iniquity': real injustice, genuine moral wrong, and it is detestable. The picture is not of a single crime but of a whole way of being - a life whose deeds are twisted because the heart behind them has first pushed God out of the picture. The passage does not spell out who the victims are; it simply names the corruption itself, and how loathsome it is. It is the family's most basic insight into wrongdoing: behind the ugly deeds lies a heart that has already decided God does not matter.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is aven - 'iniquity and trouble are within it', the wrong that dwells at the city's core. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition, evil as permanent resident. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the wrong's presence, not its root. Seat (104) is none: the iniquity is not organ-located - it fills the city, not an organ. Bearer (105) is 'the city's wicked' (inferred): the collective interior of those whose violence and strife the psalmist sees. Operation (106) resolves to none: the row records no event-verb - there is no single act, only the abiding presence of iniquity within the walls; the silence marks this as settled condition, not a deed. Target (107) is none: no object - the iniquity does not move against a named victim here; it simply resides. Manner (108) carries a value - 'within it, day and night' (inferred): the how marks constancy and interiority; the wrong patrols the walls around the clock, never absent. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing further narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'paired with trouble/mischief' - the aven is welded to the 'trouble' beside it in the verse; iniquity and mischief keep company, one pair of residents. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'iniquity and trouble are within it' - the wrong that dwells at the city's core; aven the iniquity that, with mischief, patrols the walls day and night, evil as the city's permanent resident. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the corrupt city. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the iniquity is a condition of the inner life of the city's wicked, dwelling within. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, and with no single act - because it is not a deed but a residence - iniquity abides within the city day and night, keeping company with mischief; evil read not as an event but as a settled inhabitant of the collective interior, patrolling the walls without pause. This is the family read as environment: sin as the permanent condition of a place and its people.
narratives.story: The psalmist looks out over his city and sees something worse than a passing crime wave. Violence and strife fill the streets, and day and night, on the very walls, wrongdoing and trouble go their rounds. He does not describe a single act of evil; he describes evil that has moved in and made itself at home. Iniquity is not something that happens in this city now and then - it lives there, a permanent resident, keeping company with mischief and never taking a day off. Ruin, oppression, and fraud never leave the marketplace. It is a portrait of corruption as an atmosphere, soaked into a whole community. And what makes it cut so deep for the psalmist is that the treachery reaches right into his own circle - the betrayer is a close friend. But the picture here is the wider one: a place where evil has simply taken up residence.
narratives.variation_note: One of three aven 'iniquity' readings. Here at Psa 55:10 iniquity is a resident PRESENCE within the corrupt city (no operation, manner 'within it, day and night'). It differs from Psa 94:23, where the wicked's iniquity is BROUGHT BACK on their own heads in judgment, and from Psa 119:133, where the psalmist prays that no iniquity gain DOMINION over him. The same word names evil dwelling in a place, evil repaid, and evil resisted - environment, recompense, and mastery.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is pesha - 'for no transgression of mine', rebellion named only to be denied. Type (102) is a status, here a negated one: the standing condition of guilt is claimed absent. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked, fittingly, since the reading is a disavowal; there is no root because the psalmist says there is no transgression. Seat (104) is none: the (absent) transgression is not organ-located. Bearer (105) is 'the psalmist (denying it)' (inferred): the interior of the hunted man who protests his innocence as Saul's men lie in wait. Operation (106) is 'disavowed / none present' (inferred): the event is the disavowal itself, the interior declaring it has no rebellion. Target (107) is none: no object - there is no transgression to aim anywhere. Manner (108) carries a value - 'none of his; a clear conscience' (inferred): the how marks the quality of the disavowal, a conscience that is clear; the transgression is absent as a matter of the man's clean inner standing. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'paired with the disavowed sin and fault' - the denied transgression is welded to the 'sin' and 'fault' also denied in the same breath; three words of guilt, all disowned together. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'For no transgression or sin of mine, O Lord, for no fault of mine, they run and make ready' - the protestation of innocence; the psalmist's clear conscience, that the assault is wholly undeserved, his blamelessness the ground of his appeal, the opposite of the wicked's guilt. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait, here the settled clearness of his conscience. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the (absent) transgression, and the clear conscience that replaces it, are a condition of the inner life. The full process: with no source and no organ-seat - because there is no guilt to source or seat - the psalmist disavows transgression, sin, and fault together, resting his appeal on a clear conscience; rebellion appears here only as what he does not have, the exact photographic negative of the family's usual confession. Where others own their pesha, this hunted man declares he has none, and makes his very innocence the ground on which he asks God to see and act.
narratives.story: Hunted by men who lie in wait to kill him, the psalmist makes a very different kind of statement about sin than most of these prayers do. Here he insists he has none. 'For no transgression or sin of mine, O Lord, for no fault of mine, they run and make ready.' He is not confessing; he is protesting his innocence. The attack on him is completely undeserved, and he knows his own conscience is clear. He names three words for guilt - rebellion, sin, fault - only to disown all three at once. And that clear conscience is exactly what he leans on as he asks God to wake up and look at what is happening to him. It is the mirror image of the usual confession: instead of owning his wrong, this man can honestly say there is no wrong to own, and he makes that innocence the ground of his plea.
narratives.variation_note: This is the disavowed pesha - the one transgression reading that names guilt only to DENY it. It stands apart from every other pesha: the owned rebellion of Psa 51:1 and Psa 51:3, the God-atoned transgression of Psa 65:3, the rod-punished transgression of the sons at Psa 89:32, and the far-removed transgression of Psa 103:12. Where those confess, are covered, or are judged, this one asserts a clear conscience and makes innocence, not pardon, the ground of appeal.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chatta't - 'the sin of their mouths', the enemies' guilt located in their speech. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition of the enemies, expressed in words. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the sin's location, not its root, though pride and cursing surround it. Seat (104), unusually for this family, carries a value: 'the mouth / lips' (inferred). Against the run of readings that resolve seat to 'none', this one does locate the sin in an organ - the mouth and lips, from which the cursing and lies come. The interior wrong is booked to the speaking part. Bearer (105) is the enemies (inferred): the interior of the bellowing, sword-lipped foes. Operation (106) resolves to none: the row records no event-verb - the sin is stated as a located condition ('the sin of their mouths'), not narrated as an act; the silence marks it as a standing guilt, not a single deed. Target (107) is none: no object - the sin is the enemies' own guilt, not aimed at a named victim in this row. Manner (108) carries a value - 'in the words of their lips' (inferred): the how marks the mode as verbal; the sin takes the shape of speech. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing further narrows it, no downstream outcome booked (their entrapment is willed, not filed here as this sin's effect). Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'paired with their pride, cursing, and lies' - the sin of the mouth is welded to the pride, cursing, and lies of the same passage; the guilt keeps company with arrogance and falsehood. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'For the sin of their mouths, the words of their lips' - the enemies' guilt located in their speech; chatta't the sin of the mouth, the cursing and lies that condemn them, for which they are caught in their own pride. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the enemies. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the sin is a condition of the inner life, surfacing through the mouth. The full process: from no named source but seated - rarely for this family - in the mouth and lips, the enemies' sin takes the form of speech: cursing and lies welded to pride and falsehood, a standing guilt of the interior that shows itself precisely in words, held within yet located at the organ through which it escapes. This is the family read as speech-sin: wrong that lives in the heart but is caught at the mouth.
narratives.story: Turning to look at his enemies, the psalmist puts his finger on exactly where their guilt lives: in their mouths. 'The sin of their mouths, the words of their lips' - their wrongdoing takes the shape of speech. They bellow with swords in their lips, they curse, they lie, and all of it is bound up with their pride. Interestingly, unlike most of these prayers, this one actually pins the sin to a body part: the mouth, the lips, the place the poison comes out. Their evil is real and it is inward, but it is caught at the point where it escapes - in what they say. And the psalmist's hope is that they will be trapped in exactly that pride, condemned by their own words. It is a portrait of guilt as speech: wrong that starts in the heart but is exposed the moment it is spoken.
narratives.variation_note: Among the six chatta't 'sin' readings, this one at Psa 59:12 is unique in booking a SEAT - the mouth and lips - and in placing the guilt on the ENEMIES, not the penitent. It differs from the penitent's own sin cleansed and kept in view (Psa 51:2-3), the people's sin owned for atonement (Psa 79:9), the sin God covered (Psa 85:2), and the invoked guilt of an enemy's mother (Psa 109:14). The finding is location: here alone sin is seated in a speaking organ, wrong that lives in the interior but is exposed at the mouth.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is pesha - 'you atone for our transgressions', rebellion met by God's covering. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition of the worshippers, named as atoned. Source (103) carries a span-resolved value - 'which God atones (v3)': the transgression's answer is sourced in God's own act of atonement; the sinner does not deal with the rebellion, God does. Seat (104) is none: the transgression is not organ-located - it belongs to the whole worshipping people. Bearer (105) is the worshippers (inferred): the 'our' of the temple congregation coming before God. Operation (106) is 'atoned for (by God)' (span-resolved): the event is God's covering of the transgression - notably the operative verb here is God's, not the sinner's; the interior's part is to be the one whose rebellion is covered. Target (107) is none: no object - the transgression is the worshippers' own, not aimed outward. Manner (108) carries a value - 'prevailing against them, yet atoned' (inferred): the how holds a tension - the iniquities 'prevail against' the sinner, overpowering him, and yet are atoned; the wrong is stronger than the self but not stronger than God. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no separate degree is scored, nothing further narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) resolves to none: the row books no binding partner - the transgression stands in relation to God's atonement (its source/operation) rather than welded to another interior state. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions' - the sins that overwhelm, met by God's covering; pesha the transgressions too strong for the sinner, which God himself atones, the confession that grounds the psalm's praise, sin overcome not by the self but by God. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the worshippers' condition. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the transgression is a condition of the inner life, though its remedy comes from outside. The full process: from a source that is God's own atoning act, and with no organ-seat and no coupled inner partner, the worshippers' rebellion - which overpowers them, 'prevailing against' the self - is nonetheless covered by God; the operative movement belongs to God, not the sinner, the interior's role being simply to be the overwhelmed one whom God atones. This is the family read as helplessness met by grace: sin too strong for the self, mastered only from outside.
narratives.story: This is a psalm of praise, and right in the middle of the joy comes a frank admission about sin - but with a surprising twist. The worshipper says, 'When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions.' He is honest that his wrongdoing is actually stronger than he is; it overwhelms him, gets the better of him. He cannot deal with it himself. But the sentence does not end in defeat, because the one who does deal with it is God: God atones, God covers the rebellion the sinner could never master. Notice who does the real work here - not the guilty person, but God. The sin is too strong for the self and yet no match for God. And that is exactly why the psalm can go on praising: its confidence rests not on the worshipper conquering his own sin, but on God covering it for him.
narratives.variation_note: This pesha reading at Psa 65:3 is distinctive in that the operative verb belongs to GOD - the transgression is 'atoned for (by God)', its source and remedy both booked to him, with the manner catching the tension of sin 'prevailing against' the self yet covered. It differs from the penitent's owned and pleaded rebellion (Psa 51:1, 3), the disavowed transgression (Psa 59:3), the sons' rod-punished transgression (Psa 89:32), and the transgression removed far off (Psa 103:12). Here the finding is agency: sin too strong for the self, overcome only by God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is ashmah - 'the wrongs I have done', real guilt frankly owned before God. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition of guilt, the wrongs the psalmist has done. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the owning, not the root. Seat (104) is none: the guilt is not organ-located - it belongs to the whole self. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred): the drowning-in-waters sufferer, hated without cause yet not claiming to be sinless. Operation (106) is 'done / committed' (inferred): the event is the doing of the wrongs, now acknowledged. Target (107) is none: no object - the guilt is the psalmist's own, not aimed outward. Manner (108) carries a value - 'not hidden from God' (inferred): the how marks the openness of the owning; the wrongs are laid frankly before God, concealed from no one. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) carries a span-resolved value: this is 'paired with his folly' - the wrongs done are welded to the 'folly' God knows in the same verse; guilt and foolishness owned together. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you' - the guilt the psalmist owns before God; ashmah his real faults, acknowledged frankly - his innocence of the enemies' charges does not make him sinless, and he hides nothing from God. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the honest sufferer. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the guilt is a condition of the inner life, owned within. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the psalmist frankly owns the wrongs he has done - his folly and his faults laid open, hidden from God at no point - even as he suffers hatred he did not earn; a striking double honesty, for the man wronged without cause refuses to pretend he is sinless, welding his real guilt to his folly and holding it within as something he will not conceal from God. This is the family read as candour: guilt owned by one who could have claimed innocence.
narratives.story: This sufferer is drowning in troubles and hated by more enemies than he can count, all without cause. He could easily play the pure victim. Instead he does something quietly remarkable: he admits his own faults. 'O God, you know my folly; the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you.' He does not pretend that being wrongly hated makes him sinless. He owns his real failures and his foolishness openly, holding nothing back from God. So there are two kinds of honesty here at once - he is honest that the attacks on him are undeserved, and honest that he is not without sin. He hides nothing.
