It is the candour of a man who refuses both to excuse his enemies' cruelty and to excuse himself; whatever wrong is genuinely his, he lays it plainly before the God who already sees it all.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chata - 'they sinned still more against him', sin mounting even amid the wonders. Type (102) is an action: a doing, the act of sinning, here repeated and increasing. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the sinning, not its root, though the passage shows it springing from craving and unbelief. Seat (104) is none: the sinning is not organ-located - it is the people's deed. Bearer (105) is 'they' (inferred): the wilderness generation, read from within as they test God. Operation (106) is 'sin': the event is the sinning itself, and pointedly it is 'still more' - sin compounding, not diminishing, in the face of provision. Target (107) is 'against God' (inferred): the sin is aimed at God - it is rebellion against the Most High. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree beyond 'still more' is scored, nothing further narrows it, no downstream outcome booked (God's wrath follows but is not filed here as this act's effect). Coupling (112) is 'paired with rebelling against the Most High' (inferred): the sinning is welded to rebellion; sin and defiance are one movement, the act of missing the mark shading into open revolt. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'Yet they sinned still more against him, rebelling against the Most High' - sin mounting even amid the wonders. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the rebellious generation. Locus (116) is external:god - the sin's reference-point is God, against whom it mounts; its whole orientation lies outside the self, in defiance of God. The full process: from a source the passage names but the row leaves unbooked - craving and unbelief - and with no organ-seat, the people sin 'still more', their wrongdoing increasing precisely where gratitude was due; the act welded to rebellion against the Most High and aimed wholly at God. This is the family read as escalation: sin that grows rather than shrinks in the presence of mercy, defiance mounting against the very God who provides.
narratives.story: This part of the psalm retells Israel's history in the wilderness, and it is a grim story. God had done wonder after wonder for them - split the sea, brought water from a rock - and how did they respond? They 'sinned still more against him.' That little phrase is the point: their wrongdoing did not shrink in the face of all that goodness; it grew. The more God gave, the more they defied him, testing him, demanding, doubting whether he could really provide. Their sin was not a stumble but a mounting rebellion, aimed squarely at the God who kept rescuing them. It is one of the hardest truths in the whole family of sin: kindness does not automatically soften a rebellious heart. Sometimes, faced with mercy, people only dig in deeper. Here the wonders themselves become the backdrop against which their defiance rises.
narratives.variation_note: One of five chata 'sinned' readings, and one of the two Asaph readings where sin is an ACTION of mounting rebellion against God (locus external to God). Here at Psa 78:17 the note is escalation amid the wonders - 'they sinned still more', welded to rebelling against the Most High. Its near-twin at Psa 78:32 stresses persistence past judgment ('they still sinned'). Both differ from the penitent confessions of Psa 41:4 and Psa 51:4 and the corporate owning of Psa 106:6: there sin is confessed, here it is compounded.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chata - 'In spite of all this, they still sinned', sin persisting past both mercy and judgment. Type (102) is an action: a doing, the continued act of sinning. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the persistence, not its root, though unbelief is named beside it. Seat (104) is none: the sinning is not organ-located - it is the people's deed. Bearer (105) is 'they' (inferred): the same generation, now having eaten the craved food and seen God kill the strongest among them. Operation (106) is 'sin': the event is the sinning, marked here as continuing 'still' - unbroken even after judgment. Target (107) is 'against God' (inferred): the sin is aimed at God, the one whose wonders they will not believe. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked (their days made vain follow but are not filed here as this act's effect). Coupling (112) is 'paired with not believing the wonders' (inferred): the persisting sin is welded to unbelief; the refusal to trust and the continued sinning are one condition. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'In spite of all this, they still sinned' - sin persisting past both mercy and judgment. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the unbelieving generation. Locus (116) is external:god - the sin's reference-point is God, against whom it persists; its orientation lies wholly outside the self. The full process: from a source the passage names but the row leaves unbooked - unbelief - and with no organ-seat, the people go on sinning even after judgment has fallen among them; the act welded to their refusal to believe the wonders, aimed wholly at God. Where the Psa 78:17 reading marks sin mounting amid mercy, this one marks sin surviving even punishment - the interior so set that neither gift nor blow turns it. This is the family read as intractability: sin that neither kindness nor judgment can dislodge.
narratives.story: The story gets worse. God had given the people exactly the food they craved - and then, in judgment, struck down the strongest among them while the food was still in their mouths. You might think that would stop them. It did not. 'In spite of all this, they still sinned.' Neither the gift nor the terrible punishment changed them; they kept right on in their wrongdoing, still refusing to believe what God had plainly done. This is even more sobering than the earlier scene. There, sin grew despite God's kindness; here, it survives even his judgment. The people's hearts were so set against God that nothing - not generosity, not disaster - could pry them loose. It is a stark picture of how deeply sin can dig in: a rebellion that outlasts both mercy and the rod.
narratives.variation_note: The twin of Psa 78:17: the same chata as an ACTION of rebellion against God, but where v17 marks sin MOUNTING amid the wonders (welded to rebelling against the Most High), v32 marks sin PERSISTING past judgment (welded to not believing the wonders). The difference the study keeps is between escalation under mercy and intractability under the rod - two proofs that this generation's sin yielded to neither. Both contrast with the penitent and corporate confessions elsewhere (Psa 41:4; 51:4; 106:6).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is avon - 'he atoned for their iniquity', guilt that God's mercy covered rather than destroyed. Type (102) is a state: a standing condition of the people, their borne guilt. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the guilt as atoned, not its root. Seat (104) is none: the iniquity is not organ-located - it belongs to the whole people. Bearer (105) is 'they' (inferred): the same faithless generation, whose heart 'was not steadfast toward him'. Operation (106) is 'bear guilt': the event is the people's bearing of iniquity - guilt held as their condition, now met by atonement. Target (107) is 'before God' (inferred): the iniquity stands before God, the one who chooses to cover rather than consume it. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the compassion that atoned it' (inferred): the borne iniquity is welded to God's compassion; the guilt and the mercy that covered it are held together, the wrong defined here by what met it. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity' - the guilt God's mercy covered rather than destroyed. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the people's condition. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the iniquity is a condition of the inner life, though its remedy comes from God's compassion. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the people bear a guilt that stands before God - and the reading defines that guilt not by its content but by its outcome: God, being compassionate, atones for it, restrains his anger, and does not destroy them. The iniquity is welded to the compassion that covered it. This is the family read against the backdrop of mercy: the same rebellious generation's guilt, real and borne, yet met by a God who chooses covering over destruction, remembering they are but flesh.
narratives.story: After the long, painful record of the people's rebellion, the psalm pauses on something unexpected: mercy. Their guilt was real - their hearts were not true to God, and they had broken faith again and again. But 'he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them.' The very generation that would not stop sinning was met, not with the destruction they had earned, but with covering. God held back his anger, again and again, and remembered that they were only frail flesh, here today and gone like a passing breeze. So the wrongdoing here is defined by what answered it: not consumed, but forgiven; not wiped out, but carried. It is one of the tenderest turns in the whole psalm - guilt that deserved the worst, met instead by a compassion that chose to cover it and let the people live.
narratives.variation_note: Among the nine avon 'iniquity' readings, this one at Psa 78:38 is guilt DEFINED BY THE MERCY THAT COVERED IT - real iniquity borne by the faithless, yet atoned by God's compassion rather than destroyed. It differs from the surrounding menace of the wicked (Psa 49:5), the crushing burden (Psa 38:4), the washed and inborn guilt of Psa 51, the chastened guilt of the sons (Psa 89:32), and the judgment-bearing guilt of Psa 106:43. Here the emphasis falls not on confession or content but on God's covering - iniquity remembered chiefly as what compassion forgave.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is avon - 'our former iniquities', the confessed guilt of the fathers owned by the praying community. Type (102) is a state: a standing condition, guilt inherited and borne. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked beyond 'former'; the row reports the confessed guilt, not a traced root. Seat (104) is none: the iniquities are not organ-located - they belong to the whole people across generations. Bearer (105) is 'we (the people)' (inferred): the interior of the devastated community, brought very low. Operation (106) is 'bear former guilt': the event is the bearing of inherited iniquity - the present generation carrying the guilt of those before them. Target (107) is 'before God' (inferred): the iniquities stand before God, whom they beg not to remember them. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with being brought low and the plea not to remember' (inferred): the borne guilt is welded both to the people's low estate and to their prayer that God not hold it against them; the iniquity, the ruin, and the plea are one movement. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'Do not remember against us our former iniquities' - the confessed guilt of the fathers, owned by the praying community; sin acknowledged as the deeper cause of the ruin. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the community's condition. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the iniquities are a condition of the inner life of the people, borne within. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the ravaged community owns the 'former iniquities' of the fathers as its own borne guilt - naming sin, not merely the enemy, as the deeper cause of its ruin - and pleads that God not remember it, welding the guilt to both their low estate and their cry for mercy. This is the family read as inherited confession: a suffering people looking past their attackers to their own accumulated guilt, and asking God to let it go.
narratives.story: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and this prayer could easily have been nothing but a complaint against the enemies who destroyed it. Instead it turns inward and looks deeper. 'Do not remember against us our former iniquities,' the people pray. They own the guilt of the generations before them as their own, and they name that guilt - not just the invaders - as the real reason they have been brought so low. It is a striking honesty in the middle of disaster: rather than only blaming those who attacked them, they confess the accumulated wrong of their own people. And having owned it, they beg God to let it go, to stop holding it against them, and to come quickly with compassion. It is inherited guilt frankly carried and laid before God, a suffering community asking not just for rescue from enemies but for release from its own past.
narratives.variation_note: This iniquities reading at Psa 79:8 is INHERITED, CONFESSED guilt - the 'former iniquities' of the fathers owned by the ruined community and pleaded not-remembered. Among the eight avon 'iniquities' readings it differs from the crushing personal burden (Psa 38:4), the total erasure sought by the individual penitent (Psa 51:9), the guilt exposed before God (Psa 90:8), the mercy that withholds repayment (Psa 103:10), the affliction-bearing guilt (Psa 107:17), and the Psa 130 reckoning/redemption pair. Here the note is corporate and ancestral - a people confessing the past as the ground of present ruin.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chattath - 'atone for our sins', the people's sins owned in an appeal for pardon. Type (102) is a state: a standing condition of the people, their guilt named for atonement. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the confessed sin, not its root. Seat (104) is none: the sins are not organ-located - they belong to the whole people. Bearer (105) is 'we (the people)' (inferred): the same ruined community. narratives.story: In the same breath as owning the guilt of their fathers, the people name their own sins and ask God to deal with them: 'Help us, O God of our salvation... deliver us, and atone for our sins.' What is telling is the reason they give - 'for your name's sake.' They do not claim to deserve pardon; they do not point to anything good in themselves. They rest their whole appeal on God's own reputation, asking him to act for the honour of his name. So this is guilt honestly confessed and then handed over to God, with the plea that he cover it not because the people have earned it but because it would be worthy of who he is. Together with the confession of their fathers' iniquity a line earlier, it is the full admission of a broken people: we have sinned, and our only hope is that you, for your own name's sake, will wipe it away.

narratives.story: This psalm looks back before it looks forward. It opens by remembering a time when God was good to his land - and at the heart of that memory is forgiveness: 'You covered all their sin.' The people's wrongdoing is recalled here not as a live accusation but as something God once hid completely, all of it, when he forgave their guilt and turned away his anger. That memory is doing real work in the prayer: because God once covered their sin, the people dare to ask him to restore them again now. So the guilt is named, but named as the thing grace already dealt with. It is a hopeful way to speak of sin - remembering not its sting but its pardon - and using that past mercy as the reason to plead for mercy once more.

narratives.story: Right beside the memory of God covering the people's sin stands its twin: 'You forgave the iniquity of your people.' The psalm is dwelling on the same past mercy from two angles - sin hidden, guilt lifted - because that mercy is exactly what gives the people courage to pray now. Their iniquity is remembered not as something still hanging over them, but as something God once graciously took away. And that is the whole basis of their appeal: the God who forgave them before is the God they now beg to revive them again. It is guilt spoken of in the warmest possible key - not as a burden pressing down, but as a weight already lifted by grace, and therefore as a reason for hope.

narratives.story: In this psalm God is remembering his promise to David's royal line, and he is completely honest about what will happen when David's descendants go wrong. If they forsake his law, 'I will punish their transgression with the rod and their iniquity with stripes.' Their guilt is real and it will bring discipline - a beating, even. But the crucial thing is what comes next: 'but I will not remove from him my steadfast love.' The punishment is a father's correction, not a father's abandonment. God will discipline their sin without breaking his covenant or casting them off. So the wrongdoing here is guilt met by the rod but held safely inside a love that refuses to let go. It is one of the most reassuring pictures of sin and its consequences: correction that hurts, but never the loss of the relationship.

narratives.story: Alongside the promise to discipline the sons' guilt, God names their rebellion too: 'I will punish their transgression with the rod.' The psalm keeps the two words side by side - rebellion and guilt - and answers both the same way: with correction. If David's descendants break faith, God will not pretend it does not matter; he will take up the rod. But the whole weight of the passage falls on what he then swears he will not do - he will not withdraw his love, will not break his covenant, will not go back on his word. So their rebellion draws real punishment, yet the relationship itself is never in danger. It is the picture of a father who will not spoil his children by ignoring their wrongdoing, but who will also never throw them out of the family. The rod, yes; rejection, never.

narratives.story: Moses, praying about how short and hard human life is, reaches for the reason our days pass away under God's anger - and he finds it in our sin. 'You have set our iniquities before you,' he says: our wrongdoing is laid out fully in God's sight, nothing tucked away. In the same breath he adds that even our secret sins stand exposed 'in the light of your presence.' Nothing is hidden from God - not the open wrongs, not the buried ones. And this, Moses says, is the real reason life is so brief and so full of trouble: our guilt, spread out before God, is the hidden cause of the wrath that sweeps us away like grass that withers by evening. It is a sobering thought - that the shortness of our lives is tied to sin God sees perfectly, however well we hide it from each other.

The finding is total exposure - sin that cannot be hidden from God, tied to the brevity of life.

narratives.story: Moses does not stop at the sins everyone can see. He goes after the ones we think are safely hidden: 'our secret sins in the light of your presence.' The faults we keep from other people, the wrongs buried so deep we half-forget them ourselves - all of them stand fully lit before God's face. His presence is like a light that leaves no shadow to hide in. Set right next to our open iniquities in the same line, these secret sins make the point complete: there is no wrongdoing, visible or concealed, that escapes God's gaze. It is a searching, almost uncomfortable truth - that the things we are most sure no one knows are precisely the things laid bare in the light of the God we live before.

narratives.story: The wicked in this psalm are brazen: they crush the helpless and murder the innocent, and they say to themselves, 'The Lord does not see; the God of Jacob does not notice.' The psalm's answer is that the God who made the eye certainly does see - and it ends with what he will do about it. 'He will bring back on them their iniquity and wipe them out for their wickedness.' Their own guilt is going to come back on their own heads. The evil they poured out on others will return on themselves, and God, the very one they thought was blind, will be the one who repays them. It is a picture of sin as something that ultimately recoils on the person who commits it - the wrongdoing circling back as the wrongdoer's own ruin. What they were sure no one saw becomes exactly what undoes them.

It differs from Psa 55:10, where iniquity is a resident presence within the corrupt city, and Psa 119:133, where the psalmist prays no iniquity gain dominion over him. The same word names evil that dwells, evil resisted, and here evil that recoils - the guilt returning as the guilty one's own destruction.

narratives.story: This is a psalm about God's holiness, and it makes a subtle, sobering point about the sins even of God's own faithful people. Remembering Moses, Aaron, and Samuel - people God answered and forgave - it says he was 'a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings.' Both things at once. Their misdeeds were genuinely pardoned, and yet they were not simply brushed aside; a holy God still reckoned with them. Forgiveness did not mean the wrongdoing carried no weight at all. It is a striking balance: God's people are truly forgiven, but their sins are taken seriously enough that even a merciful God responds to them. Grace covers the guilt, and holiness still answers it. The wrongdoing of the pardoned is not treated as if it never mattered.

Seat (104) is none: the iniquity is not organ-located - it belongs to the whole self. Bearer (105) is 'the psalmist / us' (inferred): the soul the psalmist calls to bless the Lord and forget none of his benefits. Operation (106) is 'have iniquity forgiven': the event is the self's guilt met by God's pardon. Target (107) is 'by God' (inferred): the iniquity is forgiven by God - the reckoning belongs to him. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored (though 'all' is named), nothing further narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'internal:ib-state', but by content the binding is with God's forgiving: the iniquity is welded to the act of forgiveness that heads the list of benefits, pardon named first among the healings, redeemings, and crownings that follow. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'who forgives all your iniquity' - the guilt God pardons, the first of the benefits not to be forgotten. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the self's condition under grace. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the self's iniquity - all of it - is forgiven by God, and this forgiveness is set at the very head of the benefits the soul is told never to forget, before healing, redemption, and crowning with love. The guilt is welded to the pardon that answers it. This is the family read as the first mercy: iniquity known chiefly as the thing God forgives, the opening gift in a catalogue of grace that the whole self is summoned to bless him for.
narratives.story: This is one of the great psalms of thanksgiving, and it begins by telling the soul to bless God and not to forget a single one of his kindnesses. Then it starts listing them - and the very first item on the list is forgiveness: 'who forgives all your iniquity.' Before healing, before rescue from the pit, before being crowned with love and mercy, comes this: God pardons all your guilt. The wrongdoing is real, but here it is named only to point to what God does with it - he forgives it, and forgives all of it. It is guilt spoken of as the first and best of God's gifts, the thing the grateful heart should remember before anything else. The psalm does not dwell on the sin; it dwells on the pardon, and puts that pardon at the top of everything the soul has to be thankful for.
narratives.variation_note: This avon reading at Psa 103:3 is iniquity as THE FIRST BENEFIT FORGIVEN - guilt named only to head the catalogue of God's mercies, welded to the act of forgiveness itself. Among the nine avon readings it differs from menace (Psa 49:5), burden (Psa 38:4), inborn stain (Psa 51:5), the exposure of Psa 90:8, and the judgment-bearing guilt of Psa 106:43. Alongside the closely related Psa 103:10 (guilt God does not repay), it belongs to this psalm's sustained reading of iniquity as the object of a mercy that is celebrated, not dreaded.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chet - 'He does not deal with us according to our sins', our failures that God's mercy does not requite as they deserve. Type (102) is a state: a standing condition of 'us', now not repaid in kind. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the un-requited sins, not their root. Seat (104) is none: the sins are not organ-located - they belong to the whole community 'us'. Bearer (105) is 'us' (inferred): those on whom God has compassion 'as a father', who fear him. Operation (106) is 'have sins': the event is the bearing of sins that God chooses not to answer as strict justice would. Target (107) is 'not repaid by God' (inferred): the sins are the thing God declines to requite - the target is that withheld repayment, mercy where recompense was due. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'internal:ib-state', but by content the binding is with God's mercy: our sins are welded to the mercy that does not deal with us as they deserve; guilt held together with the grace that refuses to repay it. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'He does not deal with us according to our sins' - our sins, which God's mercy does not requite as they deserve. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the self's condition under grace. Locus (116) - by content internal:ib-state, the sins a condition of the inner life, met by mercy. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, 'our sins' are borne but not answered in kind - God, merciful and slow to anger, does not deal with us as our failures deserve; the guilt is welded to the mercy that withholds the deserved repayment. Set beside the transgressions removed 'as far as east from west' (v12), this reading holds the negative side of the same grace: not what God does to our sin, but what he refuses to do because of it. This is the family read as mercy withheld-from-strictness: sin real and deserving, met by a God who does not give us what it would earn.
narratives.story: This tender psalm says God is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, full of steadfast love - and then it spells out what that means for our wrongdoing in a beautifully understated way: 'He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.' Notice the shape of it. Our sins are real, and strict justice would repay them in full. But God does not do that. He treats us far better than our failures deserve. It is grace described by what God holds back - the punishment he could rightly send but chooses not to. A few lines later the psalm adds the positive side, that he removes our wrongs as far as east is from west; here the point is simply that he does not give us what our sin has earned. It is the relief of a person who knows exactly what they deserve and finds themselves met with mercy instead.
narratives.variation_note: Among the three chet 'sins' readings, this one at Psa 103:10 is sins GOD DOES NOT REQUITE - failures real and deserving, met by a mercy that withholds the deserved repayment. It differs from the inborn sin of Psa 51:5 (a native condition traced to conception) and the sins pleaded un-seen and erased at Psa 51:9. Here sin is neither confessed afresh nor hidden but named as the measure of a punishment God graciously declines to give - grace defined by what it holds back.

Operation (106) is 'have iniquities': the event is the bearing of guilt that God chooses not to repay in kind. Target (107) is 'not repaid by God' (inferred): the iniquities are what God declines to requite - the target is the withheld repayment. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'internal:ib-state', but by content the binding is with 'our sins': the iniquities are welded to the sins of the parallel line; guilt named twice, from two angles, as the thing mercy does not repay. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'nor repay us according to our iniquities' - our guilt, which God graciously does not repay in full. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, 'our iniquities' are borne but not repaid in full - God declining to give the recompense strict justice would demand; the guilt welded to the parallel 'sins' it doubles. Preserving the distinction, this reading holds the iniquities not-repaid while its partner holds the sins not-dealt-with; two words for the one guilt that mercy leaves unanswered. This is the family read as spared recompense: iniquity real enough to deserve full repayment, met by a God who withholds it.
narratives.story: In the very same line that says God does not deal with us as our sins deserve, the psalm doubles the thought: 'nor repay us according to our iniquities.' It is saying the same merciful thing twice, from two angles, to let it land. Our guilt is real, and by rights it should be paid back in full. But God does not repay it that way. He knows exactly what we are - he 'remembers that we are dust' - and instead of giving our iniquities the recompense they have earned, he holds that punishment back. The two words for our wrongdoing, sins and iniquities, are named together precisely to be swept together under the same mercy. It is the picture of a father who understands his frail children and chooses, again and again, not to give them what their failures deserve.
narratives.variation_note: Paired with the 'sins' reading at the same verse, this avon holds the iniquities NOT REPAID IN FULL - the two must not be collapsed; each names one word of the guilt God's mercy leaves unanswered. Among the eight avon 'iniquities' readings it differs from the crushing burden (Psa 38:4), the total erasure sought (Psa 51:9), the confessed ancestral guilt (Psa 79:8), the exposure before God (Psa 90:8), the affliction-bearing guilt (Psa 107:17), and the Psa 130 reckoning/redemption pair. Here, with the neighbouring Psa 103:3, the note is celebrated mercy - guilt named as what God graciously does not repay.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is pesha - 'so far does he remove our transgressions from us', our rebellions put at an infinite distance. Type (102) is a state: a standing condition of 'us', now removed. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the removed rebellion, not its root. Seat (104) is none: the transgressions are not organ-located - they belong to the whole community. Bearer (105) is 'us' (inferred): those on whom God has fatherly compassion. Operation (106) is 'have transgressions removed': the event is God's carrying-away of the rebellion - the interior's part is to be the one from whom it is removed. Target (107) is 'by God' (inferred): the removal is God's act - he is the one who puts the transgressions far off. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked (though the verse names the immeasurable distance, east from west). Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no separate degree is scored, nothing further narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'internal:ib-state', but by content the binding is with God removing them far: the transgressions are welded to the act of their removal 'as far as the east is from the west'; guilt and its infinite distancing are one image. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'so far does he remove our transgressions from us' - our rebellions, which God puts as far as east from west. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the self's condition under grace. Locus (116) - by content internal:ib-state, the transgressions a condition of the inner life, now carried away. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, 'our transgressions' - our rebellions - are removed by God to an immeasurable distance, as far as the east is from the west; the operative act is God's, the interior simply the place from which the guilt is taken. The rebellion is welded to that infinite removal. Completing this psalm's triad of grace (iniquity forgiven, sins not repaid, transgressions removed), this reading holds the positive side: not merely mercy withheld but guilt actively carried away past all reach. This is the family read as removal: rebellion put so far off it can never return.
narratives.story: The psalm has already said God does not repay us as our sins deserve; now it says what he does with them instead, and reaches for the widest picture it can find: 'as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us.' East and west never meet; the distance is endless. That is how far God carries our rebellions away. This is the positive side of his mercy - not just holding back the punishment we earned, but actively taking our guilt and putting it beyond all reach, gone for good. And it is entirely God's doing; our part is simply to be the ones he lifts it from. Together with forgiving all our iniquity and not repaying our sins, this completes a threefold picture of grace: our wrongdoing pardoned, spared, and finally swept away to an infinite distance where it can never come back.
narratives.variation_note: This pesha reading at Psa 103:12 is rebellion REMOVED to an infinite distance by God - guilt actively carried away 'as far as east from west', the positive counterpart to the withheld repayment of v10. Among the six pesha readings it differs from the penitent's owned rebellion (Psa 51:1, 3), the disavowed transgression (Psa 59:3), the God-atoned transgression (Psa 65:3), and the sons' rod-punished transgression (Psa 89:32). The finding is God's act of distancing - not confession, denial, or discipline, but rebellion put past all reach.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chatta - 'Let sinners be consumed from the earth', wrongdoers wished swept from God's good world. Type (102) is a status: a standing condition, the identity of the sinner, here marked for removal. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the wish, not the sinners' root. Seat (104) is none: the sinner-status is not organ-located - it marks the whole person. Bearer (105) is 'sinners' (inferred): the interior of the wicked, the one discordant note in a psalm of creation-praise. Operation (106) is 'be sinners': the event is simply being of that condition - and the reading names it precisely as what the psalmist wishes ended. Target (107) is 'consumed from the earth' (inferred): the sinners are aimed at removal - the wish is that they be swept from the earth, the wicked be no more. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked beyond the consuming wished. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'internal:ib-state', but by content the binding is with 'the wicked': the sinners are welded to the 'wicked' of the parallel line ('let the wicked be no more'); the two are the one class the psalmist wishes cleared away. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'Let sinners be consumed from the earth' - the one discordant note in the creation-praise, the wish that evil be cleared from God's good world. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the wicked. Locus (116) - by content internal:ib-state, the sinner-condition a condition of the inner life, marked for removal. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the psalmist wishes sinners consumed from the earth and the wicked to be no more - the single dark note in a long hymn to creation's goodness; the sinner-status welded to the wicked it doubles. This is the family read as the longing for a cleansed world: sinners named not to be reclaimed but to be removed, so that God's good creation might be rid of the evil that jars against it. Read without valence-filtering, it is a wish for destruction, standing deliberately unsoftened.
narratives.story: This psalm is a soaring hymn to the wonders of creation - the mountains, the seas, the animals, the sun and moon, all sustained by God. And then, near the very end, comes one jarring line: 'Let sinners be consumed from the earth, and let the wicked be no more!' In the middle of all that praise, the psalmist wishes evildoers simply gone. It is the one dark note in the song, and it should not be softened: he is asking that the wicked be swept away, wiped off the good earth entirely. The logic is that sin is the one thing that spoils the beauty of God's world, the discord in an otherwise perfect harmony, and the psalmist longs for it to be cleared out so creation can be wholly good again. Here sinners are not people to be won back, as in some psalms, but a stain the singer wants removed - a stark, unsettling wish set right in the heart of a celebration.
narratives.variation_note: One of two chatta 'sinners' readings, and the judgment one: here at Psa 104:35 sinners are the object of an imprecation - wished CONSUMED from the earth, welded to 'the wicked' who are to be no more. It stands in deliberate contrast to Psa 51:13, where 'sinners' RETURN to God as the fruit of the penitent's teaching. The same noun names, in one place, wrongdoers reclaimed for God, and in another, wrongdoers the singer longs to see swept away - the gap between mission and judgment is the finding, and this reading is the darker pole.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chata - 'Both we and our fathers have sinned', the whole nation owning its guilt across generations. Type (102) is an action: a doing, the deed of sinning, confessed corporately. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the confession, not the root. Seat (104) is none: the sinning is not organ-located - it is the people's deed across time. Bearer (105) is 'we and our fathers' (inferred): the present community joined to its ancestors in one confession. Operation (106) is 'sin': the event is the sinning itself, now owned. Target (107) is 'against God' (inferred): the sin is aimed at God, against whom the fathers rebelled at the sea. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'external:god', but by content the binding is with iniquity and wickedness: the sinning is welded to the 'committed iniquity' and 'done wickedness' of the same verse; three verbs of one threefold confession. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'Both we and our fathers have sinned' - the confession's thesis, the whole nation owning its guilt across the generations. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the confessing people. Locus (116) - by content external:god, the sin's reference-point God himself, against whom the generations sinned. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the present community confesses that it and its fathers alike have sinned - the opening thesis of a long historical confession - welding this first verb to the iniquity and wickedness named beside it, the whole aimed at God. This is the family read as corporate, cross-generational confession: not a single penitent but a whole people owning, as one, the sin of past and present against God.
narratives.story: This psalm sets out to retell the nation's long history of failure, and it begins not with excuses but with a sweeping confession: 'Both we and our fathers have sinned; we have committed iniquity; we have done wickedness.' The very first word is 'we' - the present generation - joined to 'our fathers.' They are not pointing back and blaming the ancestors; they are owning the guilt together, past and present as one. And they pile up three words for it - sinned, committed iniquity, done wickedness - to leave no doubt about how thorough the confession is. All of it is against God, the God their fathers defied even at the Red Sea after he had just rescued them. It is the honest opening of a people looking clearly at their whole story and admitting, without flinching, that from their ancestors down to themselves they have been in the wrong before God.
narratives.variation_note: The fifth chata 'sinned' reading, and the corporate one: here at Psa 106:6 the confession is 'we and our fathers', the whole nation owning cross-generational guilt against God, welded to the parallel 'committed iniquity' and 'done wickedness'. It differs from the individual penitent confessions of Psa 41:4 (healing-plea) and Psa 51:4 (against you only), and from the Asaph readings where sin is mounting rebellion (Psa 78:17, 32). Here sin is neither a single man's fault nor an enemy's defiance but a people's shared inheritance, confessed as one.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is avah - 'we have committed iniquity', the twisting or bending of what is right. Type (102) is an action: a doing, the act of committing iniquity. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the confession, not the root. Seat (104) is none: the committing is not organ-located - it is the people's deed. Bearer (105) is 'we and our fathers' (inferred): the same corporate 'we'. Operation (106) is 'commit iniquity': the event is the doing of the wrong, the bending of the straight. Target (107) is 'against God' (inferred): the iniquity is aimed at God. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'external:god', but by content the binding is with sinning: the committing of iniquity is welded to the 'sinned' beside it; the second verb of the threefold confession, bound to the first. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'we have committed iniquity' - the twisting of the right, the second term of the threefold confession. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the confessing people. Locus (116) - by content external:god, the iniquity's reference-point God himself. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the people confess that they have committed iniquity - actively bent what was straight - the middle verb of a three-part owning of guilt, welded to the 'sinned' that opens it and aimed at God. Preserving the distinction from its neighbours, this reading names specifically the twisting of the right, an active perverting, where 'sinned' names the missing of the mark; the difference between falling short and bending crooked is itself the finding. This is the family read as active distortion: sin not merely as failure but as the deliberate bending of what God made straight.
narratives.story: In the nation's opening confession, three words are stacked up, and this is the middle one: 'we have committed iniquity.' It carries a particular flavour - not just falling short of the mark, but actively bending what is straight, twisting the right into the wrong. Where the first word, 'sinned,' pictures missing a target, this one pictures taking something upright and warping it out of shape. The psalm keeps the three verbs distinct on purpose, because together they cover the whole ugliness of what the people did: they fell short, they twisted what was good, and they did outright wickedness. All of it was against God. Naming this second word specifically, the confession admits not only weakness but deliberate distortion - the people took what God had made straight and bent it crooked. It is a fuller, more honest reckoning than any single word could give.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chaneph - 'the land was polluted with blood', defilement spreading from the deed to the ground itself. Type (102) is an action: a doing, the polluting. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the pollution, not its deeper root, though child-sacrifice to idols is its named occasion. Seat (104) is none: the polluting is not organ-located - it is the people's act reaching out onto the land. Bearer (105) is 'the fathers' (inferred): the ancestors who shed innocent blood, sacrificing their sons and daughters to idols. Operation (106) is 'pollute': the event is the defiling of the land through bloodshed - sin spreading beyond the doer to stain the place. Target (107) is 'the land with blood' (inferred): the pollution is aimed at the land - the ground itself is defiled by the innocent blood poured out on it. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'internal:ib-state', but by content the binding is with becoming unclean: the polluting of the land is welded to the people's own becoming-unclean in the next verse; outward defilement of the ground and inward defilement of the doers are one movement. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'and the land was polluted with blood' - the defilement of the land by their bloodshed. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the sin's reach. Locus (116) - by content internal:ib-state, the polluting rooted in the inner condition of the fathers though it stains the outer land. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the fathers pollute the land with innocent blood - the blood of their own children sacrificed to idols - sin here breaking its bounds and defiling the very ground; the polluting welded to the people's own becoming-unclean. This is the family read as contamination that spreads: wrongdoing that does not stay contained in the doer but seeps out to stain the land itself, an objective defilement following the deed. Read at full weight, it is the family's darkest content - sin as bloodshed that poisons a whole country.
narratives.story: This is the grimmest stretch of the nation's history. The people had taken up the idols of the surrounding nations, and it led them to the unthinkable: they sacrificed their own sons and daughters, pouring out innocent blood. And that bloodshed did not just stain them - 'the land was polluted with blood.' The wrong spread outward from the deed to the ground itself; the whole country was defiled. Here sin is shown as something that contaminates far beyond the person who commits it, seeping into the very land and poisoning it. And, as the next line makes clear, in defiling the land they also defiled themselves. This is the darkest picture of wrongdoing in the whole psalm - not a private failing but bloodshed so terrible it stains a nation's soil. The psalm does not look away from it, and neither should we: sin here is a pollution that spreads.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is tame - 'they became unclean by their acts', the defilement of the people themselves, sin as pollution. Type (102) is a state: a standing condition, uncleanness contracted. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked here, though the acts of the previous verse are its named cause; the row reports the resulting condition, not a traced root. Seat (104) is none: the uncleanness is not organ-located - it stains the whole people. Bearer (105) is 'the fathers' (inferred): the ancestors defiled by their deeds. Operation (106) is 'become unclean': the event is the contracting of defilement - the people rendered impure by what they did. Target (107) is 'by their acts' (inferred): the uncleanness comes by their own acts - their deeds are the means by which they defile themselves. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'internal:ib-state', but by content the binding is with playing the whore: the becoming-unclean is welded to the 'played the whore in their deeds' of the same verse; defilement and spiritual harlotry are one condition. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'Thus they became unclean by their acts' - the defilement of the people themselves, sin as pollution. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the defiled people. Locus (116) - by content internal:ib-state, the uncleanness a condition of the inner life, contracted from within. The full process: from no named source but caused by their own acts, and with no organ-seat, the people become unclean - their deeds turning back to defile the doers themselves, sin as a pollution that contaminates the sinner. Where the previous verse defiled the land, this one defiles the people; the becoming-unclean welded to their playing the whore in their deeds. This is the family read as self-defilement: wrongdoing that not only stains the world outside but renders the doer impure, a contamination contracted by one's own hands.
narratives.story: Right after the land is polluted with innocent blood, the psalm turns the defilement back on the people themselves: 'Thus they became unclean by their acts, and played the whore in their deeds.' Their sin did not only spoil the world around them; it spoiled them. By their own actions they made themselves impure, contaminated from the inside out. The image is of uncleanness caught like a stain - and of unfaithfulness, a people who belonged to God behaving like a spouse who runs after others. So sin here works in two directions at once: in the previous line it poisoned the land, and here it poisons the doers. Whatever they touched with their evil deeds, including themselves, came away defiled. It is a sobering truth the psalm insists on - that wrongdoing does not leave the wrongdoer clean; it makes them unclean by their very own hands.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is avon - 'were brought low through their iniquity', the guilt that sank them, sin bearing its own judgment. Type (102) is a state: a standing condition, guilt that produces ruin. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the guilt and its outcome, not its root. Seat (104) is none: the iniquity is not organ-located - it belongs to the whole people. Bearer (105) is 'the fathers' (inferred): the rebellious ancestors whom God delivered many times, yet who kept returning to rebellion. Operation (106) is 'be brought low': the event is the sinking of the people - and pointedly it is 'through their iniquity', the guilt itself the agent of their fall. Target (107) is 'through their iniquity' (inferred): the being-brought-low comes by way of their guilt - their own iniquity is the channel of their ruin. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no downstream outcome separately booked - the bringing-low is read as the guilt's own working. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'internal:ib-state', but by content the binding is with being brought low: the iniquity is welded to the ruin it causes; guilt and the sinking it produces are one movement. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'and were brought low through their iniquity' - the guilt that sank them, sin bearing its own judgment. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the rebellious people. Locus (116) - by content internal:ib-state, the iniquity a condition of the inner life that works its own downfall. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the people are brought low through their iniquity - the guilt itself becoming the agent of their ruin, sin carrying its own judgment within it. Delivered many times by God, they returned to rebellion, and their own iniquity sank them. The guilt is welded to the low estate it produces. This is the family read as self-defeating sin: wrongdoing that does not need an external punishment to destroy, because it bears its own downfall - the iniquity that pulls the sinner down by its own weight.
narratives.story: This part of the psalm describes a heartbreaking cycle. Again and again God rescued his people; again and again they went right back to rebelling. And the result is put in a striking way: they 'were brought low through their iniquity.' Their guilt was not only wrong - it was what sank them. Their own sin dragged them down. The psalm does not say God had to reach in with a separate punishment; it says the iniquity itself did the work, pulling them into ruin by its own weight. This is one of the sober truths the family of sin keeps returning to: wrongdoing carries its own downfall inside it. The people did not fall in spite of their sin but because of it - their guilt was the very thing that brought them low, over and over, no matter how many times they were saved.
narratives.variation_note: This avon reading at Psa 106:43 is SELF-DEFEATING guilt - iniquity as the very agent that 'brought them low', sin bearing its own judgment, welded to the ruin it produces. Among the nine avon readings it differs from guilt as menace (Psa 49:5), burden (Psa 38:4), inborn stain (Psa 51:5), atoned guilt of the faithless (Psa 78:38), forgiven guilt (Psa 85:2), and the celebrated-mercy readings of Psa 103. Here the note is consequence intrinsic to the sin - guilt that needs no external blow because it destroys by its own weight.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is avon - 'because of their iniquities suffered affliction', guilt that issued in sickness. Type (102) is a state: a standing condition, guilt producing bodily suffering. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the guilt and its affliction, not the root, though 'their sinful ways' is its named occasion. Seat (104) is none: the iniquities are not organ-located - they belong to the whole self of the fools. Bearer (105) is 'the fools' (inferred): those who through their sinful ways brought sickness on themselves, loathing food and nearing death's gates. narratives.story: This stretch of the psalm tells of people who made themselves ill through their own foolish, sinful living. 'Some were fools through their sinful ways, and because of their iniquities suffered affliction.' Their guilt turned into sickness; their wrongdoing worked itself out in their bodies until they could not stand the sight of food and were drawing near to death's door. Here sin is shown producing real, physical suffering - the iniquity and the affliction bound tightly together, the one flowing into the other. But this is not where the story ends. When these sufferers finally cried out to the Lord in their trouble, he sent out his word and healed them, rescuing them from the grave. So the passage holds both halves: sin that makes a person sick, and a God who heals the moment they call. The guilt brought them low, but the cry for help brought them mercy.

narratives.story: This is one of the fiercest prayers in the whole book. The psalmist has been repaid evil for good and hatred for love, and he pours out a torrent of curses on the man who wronged him. One of the sharpest is this: 'let his prayer be counted as sin.' It is a chilling wish - that when this enemy prays, even his prayer would be reckoned by God as more guilt against him. He wants the man's condemnation to be so complete that not even an appeal to heaven could get him off; the very act of praying would count against him. It stands as the dark opposite of the great confession psalms, where a guilty man begs God not to count his sin. Here a wronged man begs God to count everything, even his enemy's prayers, as sin. The psalm does not soften this; it lets the raw cry for justice against a betrayer stand exactly as it is.

narratives.story: In the same barrage of curses, the psalmist asks that his enemy be dragged into court and come out condemned: 'When he is tried, let him come forth guilty.' He wants the verdict to go against the man - to hear the sentence 'guilty' pronounced over him. Paired with the wish that even the enemy's prayer be counted as sin, it adds up to a demand for total, inescapable judgment: condemned at trial, and no appeal to heaven allowed to save him. This is a wronged and betrayed man crying out for justice in the rawest terms. He is not confessing his own guilt, as the penitent psalms do; he is calling down a guilty verdict on someone who repaid his love with hatred. The psalm records the cry without smoothing it over - the fierce longing of a hurt man that the one who wronged him finally be found guilty.

It is imprecation extending guilt back through the generations, sin invoked to cling to a whole line.
narratives.story: The curses in this psalm reach even into the past, into the enemy's family line. 'May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the Lord, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out.' The psalmist wants the guilt of this man's parents to stay on the record - never wiped away, never forgotten - so that it hangs over the enemy too. It is a startling and disturbing request, especially because it takes the very language the great confession psalms use to plead for mercy. There, David begs God to blot out his sin; here, the wronged man begs God not to blot out his enemy's mother's sin. The same word, turned completely around. This is imprecation stretched back through the generations, a hurt man asking that guilt cling to a whole family. The psalm sets it down plainly, in all its harshness, as the cry of someone desperate for justice against a cruel and pitiless foe.
narratives.variation_note: The sixth and darkest chattath 'sin' reading: here at Psa 109:14 sin is INVOKED to remain - the enemy's mother's guilt willed 'not blotted out', welded to the fathers' iniquity, both called down on the enemy's line. It differs from the penitent's own sin cleansed (Psa 51:2-3), the enemies' speech-sin (Psa 59:12), the sin pleaded atoned (Psa 79:9), and the sin God covered (Psa 85:2). narratives.story: Paired with the wish about the enemy's mother, this line reaches back to his fathers: 'May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the Lord.' The psalmist wants God to keep the guilt of this man's ancestors firmly in mind, held against him, never let go. It is the mirror image of a beautiful prayer elsewhere in the Psalms, where a suffering people beg God, 'Do not remember against us our former iniquities.' There, the plea is that God forget the guilt; here, the plea is that God remember it. The same idea, flipped into a curse. The wronged man is asking that the whole weight of his enemy's family history of sin be brought to bear against him. The psalm lays out this fierce demand for justice exactly as it stands, without apology - the raw voice of a man betrayed, calling down on his enemy a guilt that runs back through the generations.
narratives.variation_note: The ninth and final avon 'iniquity' reading, and the imprecatory one: here at Psa 109:14 ancestral guilt is INVOKED to be remembered against the enemy, welded to the mother's sin. It is the exact inverse of the corporate plea 'do not remember against us our former iniquities' (Psa 79:8). Among the nine readings it stands apart from guilt confessed (Psa 51:5), forgiven (Psa 85:2), atoned (Psa 78:38), self-defeating (Psa 106:43), or celebrated as pardoned (Psa 103:3): here iniquity is called down, begged kept in God's memory rather than released.

narratives.story: In this long psalm in praise of God's law, one verse quietly explains what all that devotion is for: 'I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.' Here sin appears only as the thing being kept away. The psalmist treasures God's word deep inside himself precisely as a guard - so that when temptation comes, what is stored in his heart holds him back from doing wrong. It is a very different note from the confessions and curses elsewhere. There is no guilt to own here and no enemy to condemn; there is only a settled, steady resolve not to sin, and a simple method for keeping it: fill the heart with God's word ahead of time. And notice the direction of it - the sin he wants to avoid is sin 'against you,' against God himself. It is the picture of a person arranging their inner life so that wrongdoing never gets a foothold in the first place.

Where Psa 55:10 shows iniquity dwelling as a resident and Psa 94:23 shows it recoiling on the wicked, here it is a would-be tyrant kept from the throne. This is the family read as the danger of mastery: sin as a power that seeks dominion over a person, and the plea to be kept from its rule.
narratives.story: This verse names a particular danger in wrongdoing: that it can take over. 'Keep steady my steps according to your promise, and let no iniquity get dominion over me.' The psalmist pictures sin not just as a wrong act but as a would-be master, something that wants to rule him, to get its grip on his life and run it. And he knows he cannot keep it off the throne by himself - so he asks God to hold his steps steady and keep any such tyranny from taking control. It fits the whole spirit of this psalm, where a life is deliberately ordered around God's word. Here the concern is staying free: not being mastered by sin, not letting wrongdoing become the thing that governs him. It is the honest prayer of someone who understands that sin, left unchecked, does not stay a small thing - it reaches for control - and who asks to be kept out of its power.
narratives.variation_note: One of three aven 'iniquity' readings, and the mastery one: here at Psa 119:133 iniquity is a would-be RULER the psalmist begs not to be dominated by, resisted only with God's help. It differs from Psa 55:10, where iniquity is a resident presence within the corrupt city, and Psa 94:23, where the wicked's iniquity recoils on their own heads. The same word names evil that dwells, evil that recoils, and here evil that seeks to master - and the plea to be kept from its dominion.

The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the psalmist weighs iniquities under God's exact reckoning and reaches a universal verdict - if God kept strict account, no one at all could stand; the marked guilt welded to the impossibility of standing. Yet the very next line turns: 'But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared.' This is the family read from the depths: guilt so total that under exact accounting every person would fall, set against a forgiveness that is the only reason anyone stands. It is the crying-out-of-the-depths recognition of universal guilt met by mercy.
narratives.story: This psalm cries out from the depths, and at its heart is one of the most searching questions in the Bible about guilt: 'If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?' The psalmist imagines God keeping a strict, exact record of every wrong - and realises at once that if he did, no one could survive the reckoning. Not the psalmist, not anyone. Under that kind of accounting, everyone would fall; the guilt is simply too universal. It is a humbling, level admission: all of us, weighed precisely, come up short. But the psalm does not leave us crushed there, because the very next line turns everything around: 'But with you there is forgiveness.' The reason anyone can stand at all is not that their record is clean, but that God forgives. It is guilt seen at its most total - and then, immediately, the mercy that is the only ground of hope.
narratives.variation_note: This iniquities reading at Psa 130:3 is guilt WEIGHED UNDER EXACT RECKONING and found universal - 'who could stand?' - welded to the impossibility of standing, and immediately answered by forgiveness (v4). It is one of a pair within this psalm with Psa 130:8 (the same iniquities met by redemption). Among the eight avon 'iniquities' readings it differs from the crushing burden (Psa 38:4), the total erasure sought by the penitent (Psa 51:9), the confessed ancestral guilt (Psa 79:8), the exposure before God (Psa 90:8), the mercy that withholds repayment (Psa 103:10), and the affliction-bearing guilt (Psa 107:17). Here the note is universal reckoning - guilt that would fell everyone, met by forgiveness.

Type (102) is a state: a standing condition of the people, now to be redeemed. Source (103) is absent - no origin is booked; the row reports the guilt and its redemption, not a root. Seat (104) is none: the iniquities are not organ-located - they belong to the whole people, Israel. Bearer (105) is 'Israel' (inferred): the community the psalmist calls to hope in the Lord, promised full redemption. Operation (106) is 'have iniquities': the event is the bearing of guilt now answered - Israel's iniquities met by God's redeeming act. Target (107) is 'redeemed by God' (inferred): the iniquities are aimed, in the outcome, at their own removal - God will redeem Israel from all of them. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked (though the verse says 'all'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no separate degree beyond 'all' is scored, nothing further narrows it, no downstream outcome booked. Coupling (112) - the source's field-value reads 'internal:ib-state', but by content the binding is with God's redemption: the iniquities are welded to the redemption that answers them; guilt and its full redeeming are one movement. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: 'And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities' - the guilt of the people, the very iniquities of v3 now met not by reckoning but by redemption. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the people's condition under hope. Locus (116) - by content internal:ib-state, the iniquities a condition of the inner life of the people, met by redemption. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, Israel's iniquities - the same guilt that in v3 no one could survive being marked - are here met by full redemption: God will redeem his people from all of them. The guilt is welded to the redemption that answers it. Paired with v3, this reading closes the psalm's movement from the depths: what began as universal guilt under exact reckoning ends as guilt fully redeemed. This is the family read at its most hopeful turn: iniquity that would have felled everyone, answered by a plentiful redemption that leaves none of it behind.
narratives.story: The psalm that began in the depths ends on the highest possible note of hope. It started by admitting that if God kept a strict record of sins, no one could stand. Now it closes with the answer to that fear: 'And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.' The very guilt that would have crushed everyone under exact reckoning is here met, not with judgment, but with redemption - full redemption, all of it, leaving nothing behind. So the psalmist calls the whole people to hope in the Lord, because with him there is steadfast love and plentiful redemption. The same iniquities that seemed hopeless at the start turn out to be exactly what God promises to buy back and take away completely. It is the family of sin at its most hopeful turning: guilt that could have destroyed a people becomes the very thing God pledges to redeem them from, entirely.
narratives.variation_note: Paired with Psa 130:3, this iniquities reading holds the SAME guilt met by REDEMPTION rather than reckoning - the two must not be collapsed; v3 weighs iniquity and finds no one could stand, v8 promises Israel redeemed from all of it. The distinction is the psalm's whole movement from the depths to hope. Among the eight avon 'iniquities' readings it differs from the crushing burden (Psa 38:4), the total erasure the individual penitent seeks (Psa 51:9), the confessed ancestral guilt (Psa 79:8), the exposure before God (Psa 90:8), the mercy that withholds repayment (Psa 103:10), and the affliction-bearing guilt (Psa 107:17). Here the note is full, corporate redemption - guilt entirely bought back.
